speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
Considering that an individual who committed a $750,000 fraud got only a one day sentence before the Quebec courts, while another individual got 8 years imprisonment for a $2,000 fraud about a week ago; considering that the big swindler is a rich businessman while the small one is only an ordinary citizen; and considering that those decisions show that citizens are not all equal before the law, the rich people being favoured, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That this House instruct the Minister of Justice to table before the House a bill aimed at establishing a specific schedule of penalties in the case of fraud, so that the sentence would be directly related to the gravity of the fraud, to see that judges impose penalties which are not based on the thickness of the swindler's wallet but on the gravity of the fraud.

subsubtopic: SKY SHOPS INVESTIGATION-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ROLE OF MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS IN GRANTING CONCESSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Can the right hon. gentleman now inform the House of the details of his rather lengthy meeting with Commissioner Nadon and other' members of the RCMP yesterday afternoon regarding the Sky Shops affair and, in particular, the conduct of any ministerial aides or other persons involved in negotiations or representations regarding Sky Shops interests?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SKY SHOPS INVESTIGATION-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ROLE OF MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS IN GRANTING CONCESSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of request made by the opposition, I had a meeting yesterday with the commissioner of the RCMP. I want to make it clear to the House that I am only reporting on this meeting in so far as it might have had any bearing on anything concerning members of my government, in other words, ministers. So far as other people might be concerned, I shall not entertain questions on that. I think the House will understand the RCMP conducted investigations. They have turned over their files to the provincial attorney general. If charges are to issue, they will come from that source. I think this indicates the wisdom of the practice of the government, and of the Solicitor General in the past, of refusing to give any details of investigations which might be initiated or which might be in course. This is obviously needed as a protection to innocent people.
This having been said, I want to say that the RCMP report to the provincial attorney general does not recommend that charges be laid against any member of the government. Any further information, I repeat, will have to wait the laying of charges, if any are to be laid, against whom and in what circumstances.

PROPOSAL THAT UNEMPLOYED BE USED ON PUBLIC WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask a question of the Minister of Finance, who has just replied virulently to the leader of the New Democratic Party concerning unemployed Canadians.
Is the minister not considering or is he not tempted to consider hiring the unemployed who are available for work and, instead of giving them unemployment insurance benefits, paying them more for the work they could do in various fields, like building the roads we need in Canada, and the public buildings which are not built because of the government's restrictions? Would it not be to the advantage of the government, the department and Canada to hire these unemployed and pay them decent wages, and thus at the same time develop the country and avoid heavy expenditures like unemployment insurance in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT UNEMPLOYED BE USED ON PUBLIC WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall point out to the hon. member that in Quebec, for instance, there were 25,000 fewer unemployed last month. Regarding supplementary expenditures for building, I must say that we have found that the government must control its expenses. That means we cannot spend more money for special programs, as my colleague the President of the Treasury Board has announced. For these reasons, we expect a resumption of economic activity in Canada this spring and summer, and significant reductions of the unemployment rate.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT UNEMPLOYED BE USED ON PUBLIC WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
The minister tells us that he must control public spending in Canada. I agree with him on this point. However, we cannot anticipate the number of people who will be unemployed next month or next week. Thus the government does not control anything at all. So my question is the following: if we cannot control the increase in the rate of unemployment-and when the minister says there were 25,000 fewer unemployed in the province of Quebec, I do not think of Quebec alone, but of Canada as a whole, and in the whole of Canada unemployment is on the rise-then I ask the minister this question: rather than not being able to control these spendings, let us pay those who are actually unemployed, that is, why does not the government consider the possibility of hiring them and paying them normal wages, which would allow to have something done, while nothing is being done right now and yet money is spent on the unemployed just the same?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT UNEMPLOYED BE USED ON PUBLIC WORKS PROGRAM

speechtext:

As the Senate report on the state of the textile industry in Canada states that the domestic industry's share of the Canadian market has been allowed to slip from 64 per cent ten years ago to less than 46 per cent now and that 25,000 textile workers were laid off in the past year and the unemployment rate among textile workers was 18 per cent in 1975 compared with the Canadian average of 7 per cent, does the government intend to follow the recommendation of the Senate that:
The minister should negotiate voluntary restraint agreements on more textile products and with more countries and these should be more closely policed than at present. In addition, the government should keep an up to date import control list so it knows what the situation is.

I also cite May's Parliamentary Practice, eighteenth edition, page 148. Not one of the examples given in that citation is similar to the matter described and put forward by the minister and complained of. The only example which is in the least similar to the matter complained of comes under the heading on page 149, "Imputations against members of corruption in the execution of their duties."
I submit that the statement of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, that the then minister of DREE was allowed input into the question of the lease, falls far short of an allegation of corruption. The then minister of transport acknowledged that he subsequently knew of the exchange of correspondence, although he had not seen it. That, sir, may be proper conduct. Again, a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the now public admission in the matter of the extension of the Sky Shops lease that the then minister of DREE was allowed input into the question as Quebec leader-
Business of the House
That is an allegation. It could not be interpreted in any other way. I find that it is an allegation. The question I now have to decide is whether it constitutes a question of privilege. I find it does not constitute a question of privilege. It is an allegation which is denied; it is an allegation which has been called false, but it is not an allegation of improper conduct. It is not unparliamentary language, and it is not in any of the confines of the definition of questions of privilege that have been accepted in the past. It is an accusation or allegation made by one member in respect of the conduct of another. It concerns an allegation of fact which is disputed. That is something that occurs rather frequently in the House.
It may constitute a matter of great irritation or debate both inside and outside the House and a matter of considerable significance vis-a-vis the reputation of members on either side of the House, but within the confines of the definition as I understand it, it does not constitute a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to the length of the present session of parliament. I realize that there is nothing in the rule books that requires the government to prorogue a session of parliament within any given period of time. However, in view of the fact that traditions are being shattered by the length of this present session, which is approaching two years, it seems that parliament ought at some point to be advised whether this session is going to go on and on, or whether the government plans for it to be prorogued within a reasonable time.
I recognize that today is Tuesday, not Thursday. However, since we will not be here on Thursday it is a matter of order that the House be told of the government's plans, not just for the next few days but for the balance of this session. Does it intend to bring the session to an end in 1976? If so, when? What does it expect the House to do between now and whatever date it plans for the session to be ended? There are two questions here: When will the session be prorogued, and when will the summer recess commence? At some point before we rise for the Easter recess the House has the right to have this information communicated to it. I realize that this could perhaps be done tomorrow on the motion regarding the Easter adjournment, but it strikes me it would be useful for us to have his information in advance of that debate. Order, please. The last time the hon. member raised this question on the same point of order, I tried to explain the situation in French. It might not have been clear. So, I must explain it once more but this time perhaps I should do so in English.

Standing Order 43 does not envisage speeches on a motion which are described in Standing Order 28. The question to which the House is asked to address itself, pursuant to Standing Order 43, is whether or not it wishes to give its unanimous consent to setting aside whatever business is scheduled for the day in order to debate something else.
Dairy Policy
A withholding of consent might constitute simply an expression of refusal to stop the debate of the day, refusal to stop the question period, or refusal to stop routine proceedings, and have nothing to do with the merits of the question. It is not a speech on the motion, and it is not an expression either of support or rejection of the motion itself. It is simply a question whether or not the consent of the House is given to stopping business at that point and addressing itself to some other matter.
Standing Order 28, which has to do with speeches, is not applicable to Standing Order 43, where the question is whether the business of the day can be set aside in order that the House might proceed to consider something else. That can only be done by unanimous consent, and if there is a single contrary voice, regardless of the side of the House from which it comes, and regardless whether the hon. member wishes to identify himself, a motion under Standing Order 43 cannot be pursued.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty at this time to announce the dairy program for the 1976-77 dairy year. Effective today, the target returns level for industrial milk has been increased to $11.45 per hundredweight. This is an increase of 43 cents per hundredweight, or 3.9 per cent, and is in line with increased cost of production. The new target returns level is determined in accordance with the long-term dairy

April 13, 1976
Dairy Policy
policy which I announced last year and which provides for adjustments equal to increased production costs.
The rate of federal subsidy for this year will remain unchanged from that of last year, at $2.66 per hundredweight. This is in keeping with the government's wish to moderate as much as possible the increase in dairy products prices in the interests of both the producer and the consumer.
In order that the target return of $11.45 per hundredweight be attained, the Canadian Dairy Commission, on behalf of the producers of industrial milk, will offer to purchase butter and skim milk powder from processors at higher prices. The support price for butter will increase 5 cents, to $1.08 per pound. The support price for skim milk powder will increase 4 cents, to 68 cents per pound.
Part of the reason for overproduction of industrial milk during the past year was insufficient control through the use of quota. The industry has no choice but to tighten its controls this year to bring industrial mild production down from its current high levels. The provinces and producer organizations, whose co-operation is essential, have recognized and agreed to this.
Taking into consideration the amount of stocks and projected demand for dairy products, the Canadian Milk Supply Management Committee, which is made up of representatives of producers and provincial governments and is chaired by the Canadian Dairy Commission, has estimated that domestic requirements are 95 million hundredweight of industrial milk for 1976-77. This will be the maximum volume eligible for the direct subsidy of $2.66 per hundredweight.
In keeping with the fact that actual shipments of industrial milk are usually somewhat less than total market share quota, and that production of industrial milk must be curtailed, the total amount of market share quota to be allocated to provincial milk marketing agencies will be 100.5 million hundredweight. Should producers ship more than 94.5 per cent of their individual quota, a levy of $8.60 per hundredweight will be charged on all shipments exceeding 94.5 per cent of quota. A year-end adjustment will be made to assure that the $8.60 levy will apply only to shipments in excess of 95 million hundredweight.
Any milk shipped in excess of individual quota holdings will have the penalty of $8.60 per hundredweight applied, and there will be no chance for refund on any deliveries in excess of quota. The levy on all in-quota deliveries has been increased to $1.35 per hundredweight in accordance with our policy.
I realize that bringing milk production in line with demand will be a difficult adjustment for dairy farmers. But to operate an effective supply-management system, producers should not exceed domestic market demands. After all, this is what supply management means.
I wish to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that dairy farmers must reduce their shipments of industrial milk now, and not starting next fall or winter near the close of the dairy year. I do not want farmers continuing along at present high levels of production and adding to our surplus only quickly to deplete their herds at the end of the dairy year

in order to avoid shipping more milk than their annual quota allows. That sort of irresponsible action would result in too few cows remaining to start off the subsequent dairy year, and possibly in a shortage of milk or milk products a few years from now.
To accomplish an early cutback in production, and yet not to overreact to the situation, I am asking the provincial milk marketing agencies to implement a monthly allocation of market share quotas to each individual producer. If a province does not establish a satisfactory system of controls, I have instructed the Canadian Dairy Commission to take whatever action it thinks is appropriate to achieve the desired goals.
One of the major areas of concern to me is the separation of the fluid and industrial milk markets. It is apparent that milk producers would benefit from a complete integration of both industrial and fluid milk markets. I believe that producers should receive equal returns for milk of equal quality, whether the milk is intended for manufacturing or fluid sales. I am asking the Canadian Dairy Commission to consult with the provincial milk marketing boards during the year to work out a program for complete integration of their fluid and industrial milk markets. This basis could provide a system for future federal subsidy programs. I am also asking the commission to review, within the framework of approved policy, other aspects of the program in their entirety.
While the year ahead will be a difficult one for the dairy producer, I want to reiterate that the government remains deeply committed to the dairy industry. The government will be paying subsidies of $253 million directly to producers and $24 million for marketing costs. In addition, product prices will be supported at $1.08 per pound of butter and 68 cents per pound of skim milk powder. To provide the necessary support, the government is increasing its loan limit to the Canadian Dairy Commission from $300 million to $334 million to finance the purchase of these products. It is also limiting cheese imports to 50 million pounds.
The Canadian International Development Agency has also been instructed to investigate thoroughly the possibility of increasing the skim milk powder component of its food aid program either through a bilateral arrangement or through the world food program in countries or on projects where it can be beneficially used. I was told just before entering the House, Mr. Speaker, that CIDA had decided to buy $20 million worth of skim milk powder, which will eliminate some of the dairy farmers' costs, etc. At world prices, this amounts to approximately 75 million to 80 million pounds of skim milk powder that the dairy farmers will not have to finance.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that good supply management is the key to the continued prosperity of the Canadian dairy industry. It remains the policy of the governement to ensure that efficient producers of milk and cream are given the opportunity to earn reasonable returns. The policy which this government has adopted for the current dairy year will ensure that these aims are met.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, upon review of this statement and upon pondering its effects for the future,
April 13, 1976

one is encouraged to strengthen one's suspicions and doubts about this government's real intention to support a domestic dairy industry with any real, continuing stability. Agricultural subsidies, and particularly dairy subsidies, benefit producers and consumers alike. This announcement once again underlines the fact that it is this government's intention to shrink, and shrink substantially, Canada's dairy industry and to continue its policy of forcing producers to get every cent of their income in the future from the market place.
This is disturbing news to producers, but it carries with it equally severe and serious implications for the consuming public. Actual returns to producers could in the future be reduced, and market prices for dairy products likely will increase and consumption could well decline. Support appears to be reduced by some $22 million-$275 million as compared to $253 million-and it is estimated that an additional $40 million will be required from the total to cover some of the administration costs, some interest costs and storage fees, of which only $24 million will be paid either by the federal government or the Canadian Dairy Commission. Thus, a considerable portion will again fail to end up at the producer level.
It should be pointed out that when the program was announced last year with its target price of $11.02-a figure, by the way, that producers did not actually receive-the cost of production was not met then. Taking into account reductions in subsidy payments, haulage, export levies, licence fees and advertising, the amount received by producers was approximately $8.76 a hundredweight, or some $2.27 per hundredweight less than the target price.
It is widely recognized that the cost of producing one hundred pounds of milk varies. However, many well-documented cost studies indicate a figure in the neighbourhood of $14. With this figure in mind, and given the support price of $2.66 a hundredweight, producers are in fact actually subsidizing dairy products to the tune of $3 a hundredweight from their own operations. Some people may ask: How can such a statement be true; how can it be possible? Let me answer them, Mr. Speaker, by saying that it is true and it is also commonplace. It is possible because the milk cheque income must be supplemented by sales of breeding stock, by sales of cash crops, and in many cases must be supplemented by off-the-farm income.
I am not quarrelling with the minister with respect to
world stocks of skim milk powder. However, the government's record in regard to skim milk powder for export sales and world food aid must be regarded as nothing less than a complete failure. Particularly at a time of surplus product, Canada's commitment remains at a shamefully low level. At a time when our domestic stocks are in a surplus position, it is unacceptable to learn that our commitment has been reduced. I am certain that most Canadians would agree that the need for world food aid has drastically increased over the past ten years. Canada's current commitment through CIDA of skim milk powder for aid is 1I * 3A million pounds less than our last ten-year average. I trust that the minister's instruction to CIDA will be more successful in the future than the past record indicates.
Dairy Policy
The minister's statement also made reference to quotas on cheese imports. Another unfortunate aspect of this government's inaction relates to the refusal to reduce cheese import quotas. Importation of cheese has risen drastically, from 31 million pounds in 1970 to 50 million pounds in 1975. This government has ignored the traditional method of calculation that is based on a five-year average. Calculated in this manner, we would have a quota of 38 million pounds, a limit much more in tune with the needs of Canadian producers and the industry. It has been indicated by a leading industry spokesman that every million pounds of chese imports results in a loss to Canadian producers of approximately $360,000. Thus, a reduction of 10 million pounds would result in savings to the industry of some $3.6 million.
I am not quarrelling with the minister about our present domestic surplus position. There are reasons for this that should be recognized, taken seriously and given full consideration. Most of the causes are not of the producers' own making. For example, we have had some excellent weather conditions during the past season. We have experienced declines in the number of exports of dary heifers, and we have had larger than normal numbers of older dairy cows still being held because of low beef prices. There are factors largely, if not totally, beyond the producers' control.
Canadian producers welcome the opportunity to compete in a fair marketplace but they cannot, and should not, be expected to compete in a marketplace filled with heavily subsidized products from foreign competitors. In addition, they should not have to stand alone against the treasuries of the European Economic Community in the world market, which is the case at the present time. The industry has requested that some special assistance be given to producers to overcome their world market disadvantage.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am certain that many of my colleagues on this side of the House will have questions. I would respectfully repeat the three suggestions or recommendations I made previously to the minister and his officials. First, the minister should continue actively to pursue the possibility of an effective supply management program at the national level as it relates to fluid milk production. Second, policy changes should create an incentive to even out year-round production. These two factors would match more closely supply with demand; thus, a reduction in surplus stocks would obviously result. Third, the government should transfer the control of import permits from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to the Canadian Dairy Commission.
The content of the minister's statement recognizes some of the difficulties in the industry. However, its success relies heavily upon the producers' ability to match supply to demand. I am confident that the producers will fulfil their obligations, but I doubt that this government will be equally successful in meeting its obligations.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering the statement the minister has just made, the only thing I can say is that it is not worse than we anticipated, but obviously it does not make the situation much better. If the farmers of Canada supplying the dairy manufactur-
12776

April 13, 1976
Dairy Policy
ing industry were to receive $11.45 on 100 per cent of supply management quotas, those farmers would be very happy. The farmers do not receive that kind of money. While it is true that as a result of the government's policies we have been able to raise the price of industrial milk by 43 cents a hundred, we have at the same time reduced the anticipated size of global consumption as a result of increasing the price of butter by five cents and the price of skim milk powder by four cents. One of the problems results from the fact that the federal dairy policy does not, through market sharing quota arrangements, allow for a longer period of time, which is absolutely necessary in designing a program to meet the needs of dairy farmers.
The minister says we can increase production per cow. A dairy farmer operates on the basis of a herd and he has to make plans before deciding how much production he should have. If this is to be changed every three months, as has been the case in the past year, there is no way the dairy farmer can remain in a healthy state. For those farmers who are producing over 94.5 per cent of their quotas there will be a reduction, bringing the return below the farm cost of production. It would be much more honest on the part of the minister if rather than saying that the federal subsidy rate will be $2.66 per hundred, he had said the subsidy would be $1.31 on quota milk. Right now there is a deduction from all in-quota milk of $1.35, which leaves the federal subsidy at $1.31, not $2.66.
If we reduced the over-quota milk and the in-quota milk, the farmer would be left with something like 20 cents a hundred for producing milk. We should be very interested in this aspect of the matter because of its great implications not only for the dairy industry but in respect of the production of beef, pork and probably poultry as well.
If the farmer is to receive something in the neighbourhood of 20 cents a hundred for the milk he ships over quota, has $8.60 plus $1.31 deducted, and has to pay a transportation cost, he will find that shipping the milk to market will cost him money. The farmer is smart enough to know that he should buy a couple of pig's or start raising some veal. In this way the farmer will have to operate the dairy production safety valve on his own.
One of our major tasks in this country is to create a dairy industry that is able to meet Canadian requirements as well as producing for the export market. If a farmer has to decide, on a daily basis, how much milk he puts into the bulk tank, and knows if he puts too much in and only receives 20 cents per hundred it will cost him money, he will then open the safety valve and move into other production. This is particularly true if the farmer has to pay a transportation charge of, say, 75 cents. He will then end up with a net loss of considerably more than 50 cents. This will result in an increased production of beef, pork and poultry products.
As the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) said earlier, dairy farmers are concerned about the deal the minister made last November in relation to the export market. I gather from the November statement that we agreed to relate 10 per cent of our total manufactured dairy production to our imports of dairy products. The $50 million we have agreed to import in cheese production represents about 5 per cent of our manufactured production. It is not difficult to envisage that we will be importing other com-

modities, bringing us to that 10 per cent range without any exports at all.
Like the egg business, we have more exports than imports. We import eggs at the full table price but we export them at the breaker trade price. We export more eggs. But this is much like the skim milk powder business; we export a considerable amount of powder, but we do so at a loss. Who accepts that loss? I suggest it is not the government, but the loss is being absorbed by the farmers themselves.
I think it behooves every member of this House, whether interested in consumers or producers, to demand of the government that we develop a much more far-seeing dairy program than this, get away from the yearly quota and make a decision concerning what we anticipate to be the needs of the Canadian public. We should meet those needs and get whatever export sales we can. This should be done in conjunction with the provinces. The province of Ontario recently signed an agreement with the minister and that province is very unhappy with the agreement: it has written a long letter to the minister outlining ten or 12 reasons why it is dissatisfied. The province of Quebec has given the year's notice that will allow it to get out of the national share quota arrangement.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Because there is not enough money. It is not satisfactory to the province of Quebec. The dairy farmers there are not satisfied. They are getting out for that reason. I am sorry the minister did not indicate that the dairy industry, through government assistance, would be able to go into the international markets through CIDA. We are quite pleased with the amount of $20 million he announced for the skim milk proposals in respect of CIDA. However, I think we have an opportunity to get into some of the other markets again. This may have to be subsidized, but it would not have to be subsidized to the amount the farmer now has to pay if he pays the two levies for in-quota and above-quota milk.
I think the farmer would be willing to make a contribution to an export levy more in keeping with the total requirements of the Canadian dairy industry. No farmer will be particularly pleased with the announcement made by the minister today. In the long run, I think we will see again, as we did last year, that when the consumer has to pay more, there is a reduction in the amount he will consume. This will be true in respect of butter, cheese and fluid milk.
I think it behooves the minister to really give some leadership in the development of a school milk program. I think it is interesting to note that a sister commonwealth provides free milk in all hotels. There is a milk bar in all the lobbies, and they provide milk in all the hotel rooms. They also provide milk in the schools. I do not think we want to interfere with the brewery industry, but surely we could get rid of the pop drink machines in the schools and put in milk. The minister is interested in this, but I suggest he has not done a very good job in selling this program to his colleagues. He should get some help from the backbenchers who represent consumers, if not the agricultural
April 13, 1976

industry. The establishment of a program which on a long-term basis will keep the Canadian dairy industry healthy is absolutely necessary for all segments of the Canadian population.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, industrial milk producers had been waiting the minister's statement since March 29. It should be particularly recalled that on March 29, during the producers' demonstration on Parliament Hill, the minister said he would make a statement on the dairy policy for 1976-77 before April 1. However, he made this statement only today, April 13. I had an inkling that the delay would spell bad news for the producers.
For several months, industrial milk producers have seen their income shrink considerably and they fear the worst for the year 1976. The producers organized meetings with their hon. members to make governments aware of their problems and during these meetings, there was a clear indication that it was at that time, and that it is still today, a political problem and that in order to maintain the producers' incomes at the 1975 level, the federal government must inject a supplement of $40 million in the economic sector. By the way, I should like to say that any government investing in agriculture makes an excellent investment because this is the basic industry of a country. As the government party claims to be on the side of power, he had to decide whether the producers would see their income reduced in the year 1976.
Mr. Speaker, speaking of power, we must be clear on this. Does government majority represent the real power or, on the contrary, is real power represented by high finance which commands the majority government to the extent that they are restricted in their financial means, which prevents them from acceding to the fair demands of industrial milk producers? People can think anything they want but it remains that the dairy industry is very important since it provides more than 300,000 jobs throughout Canada, including the producers themselves. It gives work to many truck drivers, it creates many jobs in manufacturing, packing, transportation industries and so on. It means that this industry helps the other sectors of activity of our economy.
When we talk about subsidies to support the dairy industry some people think it is the only industry that is subsidized in Canada. We often forget to evaluate how many millions of dollars in subsidies of all kinds are given to national and multinational corporations.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to underline the following point: milk subsidies are some kind of additional revenue which is beneficial to consumers. If some day the consumer is asked to pay from his own revenue the real value of such or such dairy product he will realize that it will be even harder on his budget and that he will have to spend a major part of his revenue for food.
On the producers' side if a part of the products is paid directly by the consumers and the other part by the government it does not really change the situation, provided the producer can, when selling his product, recover his production costs plus a reasonable profit margin to earn a living at least equal to that of those working in other sectors of the economic activity.
Dairy Policy
In some countries, Mr. Speaker, the government subsidize up to 75 per cent of dairy products value. It is from those countries that we import some products and indirectly the problems we now experience are caused in part by those overly massive imports.
The minister tells us that we must reduce our dairy production to get better prices. The minister should know that it cannot be controlled like a water pipe can be controlled with a tap.
Two years ago producers were asked to increase their production. They responded. Nature helping, production was excellent in 1975. Another factor that prompted producers to improve production was the drop in beef prices. More cows were kept in the herd while farmers waited for better prices to take them to the slaughterhouse.
In any event, the president of the APU and the president of the Federated Cooperative sent a letter to the Prime Minister to bring to his attention the very nature of the problem and suggest possible solutions. First, they asked for a basic price of $11.42; second, that the subsidy of $2.66 be maintained; third, that cheese imports be reduced to 39 million; fourth, that the support price be raised by $30 million and an additional budget of $19 million approved to compensate the producer who must cut down on his production.
Well, the minister's reply today is that he will boost the price of milk by 43 cents a hundredweight to offset higher production costs. On the other hand, in another part of his statement, he informs producers that the export levy will be $1.35, 70 cents more than in the fall of 1975.
In brief, the situation will be worse than in 1975-76. In 1975-76, the government spent $270 million to support producers' prices, a subsidy of $2.66 a hundredweight, and at the same time last year the levy was 45 cents a hundredweight and the basic price $11.02. In 1976-77, the government anticipates $253 million will be paid directly to producers, the subsidy will remain at $2.66, on the other hand, the levy will be $1.35, the basic price $11.45, which means that compared with the same time last year, that represents 47 cents a hundredweight less when producers asked precisely for a raise at least equal to the increases provided by the Anti-Inflation Board through Bill C-73, and the opposite happens, we will have a drop in incomes.
Well, the way things are going, I do think indeed that it will be very difficult for young people to get into farming with any hope of success. Agriculture will slow down and one day or another our production will not be sufficient and we will have to import. When a country imports too much food to satisfy its needs, it becomes dependant on others. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should not agree to a policy that is different for everyone. Because of a light surplus, the incomes of industrial milk producers are being reduced and on the other hand, as far as labour is concerned, wages are not reduced because there are 800,000 unemployed, because some people do not work. Those who do work are paid for what they do.
The same should apply to the dairy industry. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to note that millions of dollars are being wasted in various departments for all kinds of reasons. One only has to check the accounts of the Auditor General to realize that there is mismanagement in many
12778

April 13, 1976
Dairy Policy
places. When it comes to agriculture, they immediately say they cannot give more and farmers are being called a "bunch of bawlers".
People who cannot take care of their own affairs are always obliged to complain to the state. I wish these people who behave in this way would set an example by going to the country; let them buy a farm, make up a herd and show us their turnovers, which will enable us to check whether they can do better than those we are referring to today. It is a matter of simple reasoning and common sense.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we took a step backward today with this reduction of the incomes of industrial milk producers. In closing, I wish I will see the day when we can have in Canada a milk pool so that this dispute between fresh milk and industrial milk producers may come to an end. At that time, I believe we shall have a very valid solution to our problem and be able to hope that this industry will survive and that those who are involved in the dairy industry will receive higher incomes.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister giveth, and the minister taketh away. I asked a question of the minister a few months ago, and in it I pointed out that farmers this year are getting less than they did 18 months ago. That was denied, but I checked and it is true. A farmer staying within his quota-and goodness knows, without his quota he will get no money-will actually get 47 cents less than he got last year. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) says 46 cents, but I say 47 cents less.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it all depends on what the production is. The farmers agreed with this policy, and agreed to pay the storage costs, the marketing costs of this product on the world market, etc., and we put in an extra $200 million last year. We are putting in an extra $49 million this year. We are putting approximately $84 million more into the dairy industry this year than last year. The cheques of dairy farmers may be less because they are paying-and they agreed to pay-for the world distribution of the surplus product. That is what they are involved in, and that is what the levy is for. That is what the hon. member is talking about. They will have to pay the extra levy. If the hon. member thinks I am happy about that, he is wrong. This is not all my doing. It is partly their doing and also the doing of the provincial marketing boards.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: The fact is that the farmer is getting less in his pay cheque every month than he was getting last year. In order to stay within the quota, I should like to ask the minister if there is any other way-other than in fact killing off producing animals-to cut back a farmer's quota in this dairy year.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
I do not fully understand what the hon. member means by "killing off" animals. We know that there were many dairy cows which should have been called from herds last year, and they were not mainly because, as was said by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), beef prices were low, so those cows were kept in production one year longer. We estimate that there are at the present time between 150,000 and 200,000 dairy cows which should be

called from dairy herds. Whether they will be, I do not know; but we do know there is a larger number going to market at the present time because the price for kill cows is better than it has been for over two years. Good kill cows bring about 30 cents per pound. The hon. member is trying to intimate that we are giving dairy farmers less, and that the government cares less about dairy farmers. The reason I did not bring in this program before April 1 was that we were trying to work out the very best program we could.
It amounts to approximately $84 million more being put into this program. The farmers will have to pay part of that back, but they agreed to do so. The dairy farmers of Canada agreed to that kind of policy. It will create hardship for some dairy farmers; there is no doubt about that. But if hon. members are suggesting we should put in a few hundred million dollars more, they should say so.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, regarding cheese imports, we know that they have been held at 50 million pounds this year. The minister mentioned that in his statement. What happens next year? The minister says he now has a long-term dairy policy. We have asked for that for years. But will he change the rules in the middle of the game next year? Will he go back to what he originally decided upon? Just how can people make plans for the future?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Never before last year did we have an import control system. We initiated the import permit system for bringing specialty cheeses into Canada. Never before did we have that. It was hailed by dairy farmers and by the dairy processing industry as a good thing because they needed that protection. We said that we would work toward allowing increased imports into our country, but at the same time we also said we would work toward making Canada self-sufficient in its own dairy needs. That may sound contradictory, but we also made a statement to the effect that the figure will not increase above 50 million pounds this year.
We are also negotiating with the countries which are subsidizing those cheese products into Canada and trying to work out a proper program so that their treasuries will discontinue the high subsidization of some of those cheese products coming into Canada. As it stands, our cheese producers and dairy farmers cannot compete. I do not intend to allow this figure to increase, and as long as I am Minister of Agriculture I will work toward decreasing it and making sure that farmers do not have to compete unfairly with regard to these products.
These products come mainly from 16 countries, but as many as 27 countries export specialty cheeses to Canada. Some of them export in small amounts. Our processors would never process cheese in the minute quantities which are coming in, because it would not be economic for them. They have told me that with the present facilities for cheese manufacturing in Canada, the most they would be able to produce would be 75 per cent specialty cheeses.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister on more than one occasion has expressed his concern over the importation into Canada of heavily subsidized dairy products from abroad. He said at one point the government may be
April 13, 1976

prepared to take some action with respect to this. Assuming the minister is unsuccessful in persuading foreign governments who are currently subsidizing dairy products which they are dumping on the market in Canada, is the minister willing to make representations to his colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to decrease the quota of cheese allowed to be imported into Canada?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that was seriously considered. We thought of decreasing the quota from 50 million pounds to 40 million pounds of cheese a year. I work very closely with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and naturally his officials and mine are in consultation on this matter at all times. They are the ones who are trying to negotiate in this matter. The United States was successful in negotiating with the exporters of cheese to their country so that they no longer have highly subsidized cheese coming into the United States. Often the United States is pictured as having a great system of free marketing, but in fact they only allow 3 per cent of their dairy products to be imported into the country. Our country allows 5 per cent.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: What I am trying to get clear from the minister is how long he will continue to allow foreign countries to dump heavily subsidized dairy products on Canadian markets. When will the government be prepared to take action if these other countries refuse to change their policy, and when will the government decide to impose much greater restrictions on the importation of heavily subsidized dairy products into Canada?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: I think we must recognize that many of the cheeses that come into Canada are high-priced cheeses. We are negotiating in particular with countries which are exporting highly subsidized commodities to Canada. If we do not make the progress which I think we should, I will be recommending to my colleagues in cabinet that we take some other form of action to make sure that our producers do not have to compete in an unfair manner with this type of product.

which we think can be sold, and we just hope people will buy it. We know there are many uses for dairy products of which perhaps the public is not aware. speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TIME OFF WITHOUT LOSS OF PAY FOR APPEARANCE IN CITIZENSHIP COURT
speechtext:
that Bill C-311, to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act (time off without loss of pay for appearance in Citizenship Court), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-311 is a very short bill which would add just one new clause to the Canadian Citizenship Act. I think I could best indicate what the new clause would do if I were to read its actual wording, which is as follows:
An applicant for a certificate of citizenship who is required under any of the provisions of this Act to appear before the court, when such applicant is regularly employed during the time he is required to appear, shall be granted by his employer such time off work, up to a maximum of three hours for any one appearance, as may be necessary to enable the applicant to appear before the court, and no employer shall make any deduction from the pay of any such employee nor impose upon or exact from him any penalty by reason of his absence from his work for the length of time specified in this section, provided that the absence is for the purpose specified herein.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that those words as set out in Bill C-311 are proposed by the bill to be made a new section 29.1 of the Canadian Citizenship Act. The only change that would have to be made relates to the question of where that new clause would be inserted. As hon. members are aware, a new Canadian Citizenship Act is under way, Bill C-20; indeed it will be under debate later today.
When I suggest that the new clause be numbered 29.1, that is in relation to the act as it now stands. After all, I have no alternative but to seek to amend the law as it stands; I cannot at this point propose to amend a law that has not yet been passed. Offhand I would say that perhaps the best place to put this proposed clause in the new bill would be following clause 26. In other words, if it were made section 26.1 instead of 29.1 it would fit in the new bill quite appropriately.
I suggest that the idea contained in this bill is one of those good ideas-call it a motherhood provision if you wish-to which no one can really take any objection. Despite the difficulties that private members have in this hour with their bills, I hope that this bill will be looked upon sympathetically. Certainly I would have no objection if instead of passing the bill as it is, the House would refer the subject matter to the appropriate committee, but I hope that the House will be quite ready to accept the idea itself.
I have borrowed the idea from the Canada Elections Act. As all hon. members are aware, there is a provision in that legislation that permits an elector on election day to have a certain amount of time off work without loss of pay in order to enable him to cast his vote in a federal election. If-and I am sure we do-we regard the applying for and obtaining of Canadian citizenship an important matter, I think that those persons who take this step should be encouraged to go through with it, should be encouraged to appear before the court when they have to make an application, and should be encouraged to appear before the

court when their citizenship certificate is granted. In some cases this does present a hardship, namely, that pay is lost. In the case of the Canada Elections Act, of course, we made a provision that could apply quite often in a person's lifetime. Here we are making a provision that could apply only once in a person's lifetime.
So, Mr. Speaker, I present the idea to the House. I do not think it needs to be argued at length; it is a very simple proposal. I have read the whole of the clause. As I say, the proposal is quite direct, namely, that applicants for citizenship who have to appear before a court of citizenship for any reason should be given up to three hours off work without loss of pay in order for them to make that appearance.
In the explanatory notes to the bill I have explained what it does, but I have this sentence at the end:
It is felt that persons seeking Canadian citizenship should be granted this recognition of the importance of the step they are taking.
That is the way I feel about it, Mr. Speaker. Applying for and obtaining citizenship is an important step, and this bit of recognition is well worth the favourable consideration of the House of Commons. I hope the House will pronounce favourably on the idea during this private members' hour.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TIME OFF WITHOUT LOSS OF PAY FOR APPEARANCE IN CITIZENSHIP COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has drawn to our attention a financial difficulty that may be faced by some applicants for citizenship in Canada. The question he has raised is well worthy of our attention-the possible financial cost of taking time off from work to appear before a citizenship court in the course of acquiring Canadian citizenship. He has said this is a very important step in the life of an applicant, as indeed it is. It is taken once in a lifetime. It is a very solemn moment not only for the applicant but, indeed, an important moment for all citizens of Canada. The hon. member has suggested we should give some recognition to that importance. I am going to argue that the government and the Parliament of Canada have given very great importance to that moment and, in fact, have taken more appropriate means than those suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to cope with what may be for some a financial difficulty.
The hon. member proposes that employers be required by law to grant up to three hours in time and pay for any one appearance by an applicant for citizenship. He suggests that such a requirement in our law would be similar to the requirement in the Canada Elections Act regarding time off and pay regulations. I think this is very different from that circumstance, as I will attempt to show in the course of my remarks.
While the hon. member's objective of removing any possible serious financial obstacle is a desirable one, the means proposed do not appear to me to be necessary nor, indeed, appropriate, and may in fact be of doubtful constitutional validity, although it is not on that latter point that I would rest my argument.
Other means have been developed and are in the course of being developed to accomplish the same thing; that is, to alleviate possible financial difficulties and to do this in a
April 13, 1976

way that does not transfer the burden to the employer. We should, therefore, assess rather carefully what appears on the surface to be an attractive proposal. We should assess how difficult or serious the problem is and whether it can be resolved better in some other way, as I believe it can, and whether in fact it is being resolved better in some other fashion, as I believe it is.
Under the present act, an applicant for citizenship must go to the office of the citizenship court on three occasions. He must go first to make an application and this involves documentation. On the second occasion, the applicant attends a hearing before a citizenship judge and this involves an assessment of whether the applicant meets the requirements of the act. On the third occasion, the applicant attends a presentation ceremony during which he or she takes the oath of allegiance.
The time-frame mentioned in the hon. member's bill is undoubtedly appropriate and covers any one or all of these three occasions when the applicant goes before one of the offices of the court, that is to say, three hours. Some of these occasions may be over within 15 minutes and some may in fact extend for roughly three hours.
What is being done currently to face up to the possible problem raised by. the hon. member? Over the past three or four years the Department of the Secretary of State has developed an outreach program to meet the very problem raised by the hon. member, as well as to encourage landed immigrants to come forward with applications and to take that very important and solemn step of becoming a citizen of Canada. The outreach program consists of three services: first, storefront offices, second, mobile teams of examiners; third, night courts. One could add a fourth, the practice of the courts of scheduling appearances by appointment or arrangement. In addition to these outreach services, which I should like to describe at greater length, there are 15 citizenship courts in Canada and some 12 sub-courts to meet the convenience of applicants.
Let us consider for the moment the outreach services. The storefront offices have been established in the centres of greatest pressure, that is to say, in Toronto and Montreal where there are now four such storefront offices. They are open in the evenings and on weekends when applications for citizenship can be made. If the demand arises, the Department of the Secretary of State is prepared to extend these storefront offices to other locations; that is, the applicants can meet that first occasion or appearance where the pressure has been the greatest and where the demand is the greatest, and they can do that in a manner which does not involve loss of work time or pay. There are now four mobile teams of examiners operating in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Hamilton. In these four cities some 78 per cent of all applications are currently received. These mobile teams also take applications in such prearranged locations as schools, community halls, places of work, and so forth.
These two services enable applicants to make their application at times convenient to them, with no loss of time whatever. They are available in cities where over three-quarters of citizenship applications are currently being received. Again, it is a service that may be extended if communities seek it, if volunteer organizations ask for it and demonstrate a need. These two services of the outreach
Citizenship
program are in fact being used, so it is evident they are responding to a problem of the kind raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre but in a different way from that which he has proposed.
For example, in the most active of these storefront offices, the Dufferin Street store in Toronto, last year-and the office was open, I think, for only six months-some 12,536 applications were received. This represents something under one-fifth of all applications in Canada. They were received either during the day, if convenient, in the evening or on weekends without requiring any loss of work time to the applicants.
The two storefront offices in Montreal handled about one-quarter of the applications in that city; over 5,000 out of over 18,000 applications. The mobile teams in Toronto, in 1975, took over 2,400 applications-and this is a service which is still in the early stages of development. So these outreach services are in fact supplying an answer to a certain need, not only financial but of convenience.
In addition to the storefront offices and the mobile teams, the department has tried to respond to needs by establishing night courts, again to avoid inconvenience and unnecessary financial hardship. These night courts have been established mainly in Toronto on an experimental basis in response to an initiative taken in the community of Toronto. The night courts are not for applications but for hearings and for ceremonies, the other two occasions when applicants go to the offices of the citizenship courts.
Moreover, it is now practice in respect of citizenship courts to arrange appointment times for these hearings for applicants to avoid the situation where persons have to attend and wait for extended periods of time in a line-up. This meets the need of those who may be on shift work. Persons ask for the most convenient times for an appointment and arrangements are made. These night courts and arranged appointments should alleviate the kind of problem raised by the hon. member
Again, this is a service the department is prepared to extend to other communities should a request for such arise. It is perhaps natural that the request should have arisen first in Ontario, where over half of all applications occur, and that the first response would be made there because of the activity of voluntary associations which requested it. Such activities are open to other communities which wish to seek the same thing without, as I say, the necessity of passing a law of parliament which would place the cost on the employers of those applicants for citizenship.
Some problem may remain in respect of the visit to the court for the citizenship ceremony. However, this to some extent has been alleviated by the night courts in Toronto and by night courts which have in fact been held in other cities, although not as frequently as in Toronto but, again, in response to community pressure and requests. To the extent, therefore, that a problem may remain, it seems to relate rather to the state of the community organization and voluntary community association activity rather than to the absence of a means to respond. Some exploration, in fact, of the remaining problem in respect of the night courts is presently under way in Montreal. The department

There is a certain other argument which I think should be raised in this House relative to points made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I refer to the possible constitutional problem with regard to his proposal. His proposal, if adopted, might in fact be applicable in law only to companies which lie in the federal jurisdiction. It may be, if adopted, that it will not be applicable to companies that have been incorporated under provincial law and lie in the field of provincial jurisdiction.
In addition, I think the hon. member cannot argue that the granting of citizenship ranks in the same order or measure as general elections which establish this very parliament. The elections establish the government of the country. It is obviously an essential national process. It is a requirement of our constitution that elections be held at least every five years. It is a democratic need that all citizens be able to participate. It is very difficult indeed to extend that need to the citizenship process, which is an individual choice, an individual act which occurs once in a lifetime, important as it is for all of us. It is extremely difficult to extend that argument to Canadian elections to the circumstances of citizenship applicants. It is more a matter of convenience to the case of the hon. member, but it really weakens his case because of the doubtful constitutional validity on which it rests. There is a very evident difference between a general election and the taking of citizenship.
Mr. Speaker, I would simply say this is an important problem. The problem is being met partly by means already developed and by means which are capable of extension by a department which took the initiative to meet this problem in innovative ways and is trying to bring the citizenship process to the people. This is a process which can be extended by community action in other cities in a better manner than through statutory or legal action by this parliament which in any case would be of doubtful constitutional validity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset permit me to establish my position. I will be opposing Bill C-311 because I do not feel we should have to pay people to become Canadian citizens. Certainly it would almost appear to be a shame for me this afternoon to have to oppose a private member's bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a gentleman whom I respect greatly as a member of this House. Ever since I came here as a new member I have had great admiration and respect for the proposer of Bill C-311. However, as I shall demonstrate in my remarks I do not feel this to be a wise move or one in which the government should be involved. It would place an additional burden on the employer by requesting that he expend additional funds to allow persons desirous of becoming Canadian citizens time off from their duties.
During the vote this afternoon I had time to reflect on the fact that since it is so rarely that the New Democratic Party votes against our government, it is almost a shame that I have to speak against Bill C-311 as proposed by the

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a member of that party.
However, one does wonder from time to time, when this type of suggestion is made in the House, whether it might just be another thread of the socialist fabric that we sometimes see appearing on the scene in Canada. Let me say, on behalf of the Liberal Party, that the buck stops here and we do not endorse or support this type of program. On the contrary, I would say we should be emphasizing and encouraging the necessity for greater productivity in this country. We have acknowledged and accepted our responsibility in this regard in this time of restraint. The restraint legislation, by the way, as stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other authorities throughout the country is working, contrary to some of the mutterings by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and members on the other side of the House. However, it is always somewhat amusing to me to hear recommendations from the opposition parties for the spending of more money, or the spending of someone else's money, to be more precise.
Bill C-311 asks for a contribution of money to persons who aspire to be Canadians. That money will, of course, be spent by someone other than the New Democratic Party. It will be spent by employers and by people who will have to carry the burden.
Hon. members who have travelled throughout the world know only too well the feeling of pride one has on returning to one's native land. We acknowledge that pride when we think of the freedom, the good life, the prosperity, the availability of medicine and education, and all the excellent facilities and programs which are available to Canadians. I am hard put to understand why we should entertain Bill C-311 under which we would be reimbursing prospective Canadians.
I suppose it could be said, after listening to some of the allegations and innuendos from the other side of the House, that this could almost be considered a form of a bribe to entice an individual to become a Canadian. Perhaps that is an exaggeration, but there are some who have this type of warped mentality, and sometimes we witness it in the House.
However, if we consider this proposition, we would not want to support Bill C-311 because we would be encouraging a situation where we might be accused of offering some sort of incentive, which I suggest might be called a bribe, for someone to take on the great honour of becoming a Canadian citizen.
If we are going to encourage law, order, peace, security, and justice in Canada, as is the case we hope with the New Democratic Party, I think we should be urging programs which will encourage people to respect authority, to respect police, and to respect teachers in schools. That is the type of program we should be supporting, and we should not start new Canadians who are coming into the country and who want to become Canadians off on the wrong foot by giving them the impression that this is the way it works in Canada. They should not be given the impression that they can be paid to become Canadian citizens.
April 13, 1976

I think this is a weak proposition. It would only foster an attitude on the part of prospective Canadians that this country is weak and that everyone is paid or rewarded with money to do certain things. I believe anyone who sincerely wishes to become a Canadian, who meets all the criteria, who takes it upon himself to qualify and who takes the necessary steps to become a Canadian, should not in any way expect to be paid to do this.
When we consider the amounts of money which have already been expended by Canadians for citizenship courts, subcourts, store fronts and mobile teams operating across this country, together with other services rendered to prospective Canadians, surely we should not be asked to pay a potential Canadian to become a Canadian.
There are many people in my constituency who are from foreign countries and who have become Canadians. A good many of them are in the professions and would not expect to receive remuneration or monetary rewards for becoming Canadians. Those whom I have had occasion to befriend and with whom I have become acquainted have taken their places in Canadian society. In one particular family I can think of, the son is now a general practitioner in Halifax, and the daughter is a dietician. These people came to Canada and accepted it with all its beauty and opportunity. At no time did they expect any reward to be held out to entice them to become Canadians. They made the decision and sincerely wanted to become Canadians.
Once in private members' hour when one of my colleagues introduced a bill which would have involved the expenditure of money outside this country-I refer to the bill proposing construction of a road corridor in the United States-I was convinced then, and I still am, that it was my duty to speak against that bill because of the need for the upkeep and construction of highways in our own country, particularly with regard to the situation in my riding in New Brunswick. I found it necessary to speak against that bill, and I understand there will be another similar private member's bill soon, one which we expected to be before the House last week. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) introduced that bill with respect to the proposed construction of a tunnel between Dartmouth and Halifax. I will attempt to be placed on the roster to speak against that bill because adequate moneys have already been expended in that area, something to the tune of $80 million, for existing bridges. I do not see any need for a tunnel. What I am leading up to is that when I see the type of proposition contained in Bill C-311, I am convinced that we must discourage it because it would be poor legislation.
In the time afforded to me I have expressed my disagreement, but I also wish to profit from this opportunity and to go on record, as a new member in this House, to say that notwithstanding my disagreement with Bill C-311, I have the utmost respect for the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

I fully understand the best intentions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but somehow I believe that a measure such as this one would cheapen the whole concept of the acquisition of Canadian citizenship, and I will explain why. Over the past 10, 15 and 20 years good employers have had a sense of pride in being Canadian and have done what the hon. member is proposing here today. So in that sense the proposal has already been adopted by people who are usually regarded as good employers. Those who are lousy employers-excuse that expression, Mr. Speaker-still do not recognize this fact and withhold the wages or salaries of those who go to acquire Canadian citizenship.
In order to meet these situations, which unfortunately still occur but which are rapidly disappearing, which arise because of these bad employers who are so narrow minded that they do not see that the day when a new Canadian acquires his citizenship is a day to celebrate, and therefore requires that recognition on the part of the employer who will say, "All right, Pasquale, or Joe, or whatever, go down town and get your citizenship; this is our way of recognizing this great day in your life", the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has carried out a number of additional measures which were already so clearly and effectively outlined by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell).
Our hope on this side of the House is that these programs, such as Outreach, Storefronts, and the other fancy names that go with them, will not be limited only to large metropolitan centres like Montreal and Toronto but will also be implemented in centres such as cities in western Ontario where a large number of new Canadians live, and where services of this kind would be most definitely well received. There would probably be a constant need for

them for a number of years to come, not only in southwestern Ontario but also in the west and perhaps in the east.
When listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I could not help asking myself-and I must say in advance that my thought was not totally serious-why should there not be a bill that would legislate compensation for loss of wages when a person goes out to get married? Indeed, why not? The day you become a Canadian citizen is almost like your wedding day. You have decided that your relationship with your motherland should evolve into a new relationship with the country of your choice, namely, Canada, to which you are in a way becoming married on the day on which you acquire Canadian citizenship. I am the first one to admit that the similarity is somewhat shaky, nevertheless it has some validity because it is an event of such importance in an individual's life. Therefore to talk about loss of pay on such a day does not do justice to the event itself and to the idealism of the person who decides to become a citizen and therefore is ready to give up certain hours and a certain amount of income, and in fact even pays a $20 fee for the fine privilege of becoming a Canadian citizen.
Let us look at something greater than just money, particularly in the process of acquiring Canadian citizenship.

Many new Canadians came to the east, central Canada, and the west before the first world war, between the wars, and after the second world war. Many never acquired command of or fluency in one official language, let alone adequate knowledge of it. They have not learned the capital cities of provinces or the lengths of certain rivers, but functioned well as citizens in their communities. They have raised families, sent children to school, respected the law, paid taxes, and been active in church and secular associations in their community. Mr. Speaker, I shall try to be brief and allow other hon. members time to speak. Frankly, this proposed measure reminds me of the Canada Elections Act. This is an urban-oriented, you might say union-sponsored type of bill. It is like a fringe benefit under some wage agreement. What about the man from Spirit River who must go to Grande Prairie? His journey will take a whole day. He must be prepared to take the whole day off.
I agree with something the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said. Canadian citizenship is an important matter. Yet coming out of his mouth some of the things he said sounded strange, as did the applause of the hon. member's colleagues. Tonight we shall debate Bill C-20, which will provide for the downgrading of the citizenship ceremony. It says that in many instances the ceremony can be performed across a desk. The bill removes the discretion of the judge in the citizenship court. The grant of citizenship will become an act of ministerial administration. What utter nonsense! I hoped that the hon. member for Davenport would insist on the dignity of the ceremony in court when new Canadians, in open court, before fellow citizens and friends, renounce their allegiance to their countries of origin.
I have participated in more citizenship court ceremonies than any member of this House. Since citizenship courts came into being I have made it a regular practice to appear in citizenship court ceremonies in Edmonton. One must be impressed at the attitude with which candidates for Canadian citizenship approach the final ceremony. One sits with great pride alongside the president of the court, on the bench, and sees the emotion, in young and old, when people go through the ceremony. One sees people who have been here above 40 years and now wish to take out Canadian citizenship. With great pride they repeat after the president of the court the oath of allegiance. I fear that, deliberately, we shall downgrade that ceremony.
I join hands with the hon. member for Davenport in saying that a man will be compensated in many cases if he will make this voluntary gesture affecting his status. But nobody is going to pay the Dutch farmer who must travel many miles to Edmonton from some outlying area. Farmers will not get paid. Why should anybody else get paid for this sort of thing? Why should anyone be paid, by law, for an exercise in good Canadian citizenship? I agree with the hon. member for Davenport. I think the reasonable employer will be the first to encourage the employee to take out citizenship as soon as possible. Only the most hardhearted employer will refuse his employee time off; and frankly he should be publicly criticized for his attitude. Or the employer will refuse when a collective agreement is narrowly interpreted by the business agent of a union. In those cases the employer will react in the same way.
Normally when a husband and wife want a little time off in order to sign papers for purchasing a house, the average employer says, "Surely to goodness the enlightened employer will give his employee time off to do these things. If in some industrial cities there are to be special night sittings of the citizenship court, that too will be a good way of doing it.
