speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take too much time. We have already discussed this bill in some detail when it was before the House at second reading. However, I want to express a few reservations about some of the inadequacies which surround the bill.

April 13, 1976
Quarantine Act
When the bill was first presented in the House, the parliamentary secretary indicated that it was largely to allow Canada to prepare for two large international events to be held in Canada this year, namely, the Habitat Conference in Vancouver and the Olympic Games in Montreal. Strangely enough, when the parliamentary secretary appeared before the committee, and indeed others, they tended to deny that this bill had anything to do with these two major movements of people in and out of this country in one year. It struck me as rather strange that, for some reason, they were afraid to tell us that this bill is going to have a significant bearing on these two conferences or, vice-versa, that these two conferences had a significant bearing on the bringing forward of this bill.
The bill proposes to give the minister and his officials some extraordinary powers to detain people at the port of entry, or anywhere within this country, if they have sufficient reason to believe those people may have been exposed to some communicable disease, whether it is one listed in the international agreement or some other one which is not listed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext: They are going to find many.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO DANGEROUS DISEASES
speechtext:
That is right. I was not satisfied with the explanations provided by the parliamentary secretary. Indeed he was somewhat reluctant to let the officials speak on this bill in committee and insisted on answering the questions himself. I must say I was not all that confident in his expertise on these matters.
It appears that one of the diseases which the government seems to be worried about is the one known as Lassa fever, a virus disease found largely in west Africa, generally along the southern portions of the Sahara Desert. We found from testimony before the committee that Canada has a number of people involved in CUSO working in these regions. I am quite concerned about the fact that there does not appear to be adequate protection for those working in that area, particularly because of the lack of proper facilities for treatment, and indeed for isolation, and perhaps for some other reasons.
A couple of years ago Canada made an application to the World Health Organization to have Lassa fever placed on the list of communicable quarantinable diseases for international purposes. The World Health Organization rejected this application. They said in no uncertain terms that the reason, which was based on the advice of many experts, was that quarantine as far as is known is of no value from the point of view of containing the spread of this particular disease.
We also discovered during the investigation of this bill that even if we wanted to quarantine those whom we suspected of having been exposed to Lassa fever, and perhaps of having Lassa fever in the early stages as they come into this country, we do not have the facilities in which we could safely quarantine them. This is a matter of great concern to me because the approach we are using here is not to try to prevent people from coming but to delude ourselves that we can look after them once they get here, isolate them, and thus protect our own population. This happens to be a completely erroneous assumption.

The fact is that if someone comes into this country with that disease we have no way of protecting the people of Canada from it simply because it is not amenable to containment through quarantine. It is my impression that the officials of the Department of National Health agree with that proposition. I believe we should be looking at something different.
If we are concerned about that disease being brought into Canada perhaps we should consider the possibility of not allowing people to come here if they have been exposed to it, or if we have reasonable grounds to believe they may be carriers. I am not satisfied the government has considered the possibility of excluding these people rather than allowing them to come and pretending that we can isolate them safely, when in fact we cannot. Both Britain and the United States go much farther in this direction than we presently do. For example, those countries reserve the right to prevent arriving passengers from disembarking from aircraft. Suspected cases are sent back to their country of origin which then has the responsibility of dealing with them.
As to our own overseas workers it would appear from evidence given by a representative of CUSO that some of them are presently exposed to unusual danger and that the Government of Canada is taking virutally no steps to protect their health. There seems to me to be some confusion as to what should be done if one of our workers in Africa acquired Lassa fever

whether he or she would be treated there or brought home. No one was able to tell us in the committee what would happen, and I think that was rather a poor showing. It seems to me the people of Canada deserve an explanation of what the contingency plan might be. The CUSO workers themselves deserve some kind of reassurance and a clear-cut statement on what they can look forward to if they should contract this disease. There was a suggestion that an educational program might be aimed at people working in this area designed to enable them to increase their ability to protect themselves. This might be useful, but as far as I can gather there is no such program in existence at this time.
We are left then with a situation in which the government proposes changes in the Quarantine Act. I have no objection to the changes which are proposed, but I do object to the fact that the government is basing the case for those changes on the premise that the legislation will protect the population from strange and unusual diseases whereas, as I say, it will simply not do that. We know from our experience with Lassa fever in particular that workers involved in a facility where a patient is held acquire the disease themselves at a fairly high rate, whether they are attendants on the ward or laboratory workers trying to isolate a virus. So while we do not object to the passage of this legislation-it could be useful in many ways-we are expressing reservations about the government's lack of action with reference to certain specific diseases which were mentioned during the course of the study of this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (for Mr. Jarvis) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
motion No. 1:
That Bill C-20, an act respecting citizenship, be amended in Clause 5
by
(a)	striking out the word "and" in line 38 at page 4
(b)	striking out line 42 at page 4 and substituting the following
therefor:
"section 18; and
(/) in the opinion of a citizenship judge, is not shown to be of other
than good character."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in addressing the House on the report stage of this bill. We have been through the committee stage, and again it was an experience of mixed ennui and surprise. The surprise stemmed from the fact that the minister chose to introduce a number of amendments at the committee stage which we had not anticipated. Certainly I am not critical of some of the amendments that have been made which were very necessary. Others were housekeeping and simple editorial amendments. For example, I will commend him for closing the loophole in regard to deportation orders.
Another very substantial change to the bill deals with assigning jurisdiction to the provinces for land ownership in the case of non-resident aliens. I think this is a much needed amendment, one that needed to be dealt with since this has become a matter of great concern all across Canada.
It was also an experience in ennui in that we had a repetition of what occurred when we were dealing with Bill C-58. Again the minister very tightly organized the number of witnesses who were to appear. In this case something like four witnesses were allowed to appear before the committee. None of the witnesses whom members of opposition parties wanted to appear before the committee were allowed to appear. I remember specifically the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) recommended to the committee that we hear one of the judges, but this raised the hackles of government members. We could not by any means offend any of the regulations, even
Citizenship Act
though it had already been pointed out that a precedent in this regard had been set. Therefore some of the people who could have given us a wealth of experience, information, and sound guidance in discussing the amendments were kept out.
Still the government blithely keeps repeating that it wants legislation that is in the best interests of all Canadians. As I say, Mr. Speaker, under a pre-structured committee system where government members are asked to vote preferably without thinking about what they are voting on, and where opposition members are not allowed to bring in any suggestions that would at all disturb the neat orderliness of the minister and his members, it was once again an exercise in ennui.
As is his custom, the minister gave us a copy of the statement that he presented to the committee, which I appreciated because it gave us an opportunity to deal in a concrete way with his point of view. It also gave us an opportunity to review the amendments that he was presenting, as well as some of the original provisions of the bill.
In addressing myself to the bill I want again to deal with what the minister said. I might add that the amendments, he presented to the committee during committee stage made the bill, in the language used in this House, not substantially the same as it had been but very substantially different. The minister began with one of the arguments that has been a concern of members on both sides of this chamber. He said:
It-
That is the bill.
-clearly lays down certain steps the applicant must follow and certain qualifications the applicant must satisfy. Upon satisfaction of those conditions, then citizenship should follow as a right.
The operative term used by the minister there, one that expresses his philosophy, is that citizenship is a right. There is where I disagree violently with the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). I would point out that if citizenship really is a right, then it contradicts the bill itself. The Canadian Citizenship Act provides an elaborate procedure whereby a prospective citizen has to come before a quasijudicial board and a judge in order for his case to be heard, and by that process become a citizen. Yet the minister says that upon satisfaction of certain conditions that are laid down in the act, citizenship shall follow as a right. In other words, it is an automatic process.
The most obvious question we must ask ourselves is this: if all one has to do is to meet the qualifications on the application form for citizenship and the criteria that the minister has laid down before citizenship follows as a right, why do we need a citizenship judge in the first place? Why go through the judicial system to provide citizenship for our immigrants? As I have said, it is a contradiction in terms.
When I was serving on the special parliamentary committee on immigration, commonly called the green paper committee, I remember very clearly that one of our witnesses was the chairperson of the Immigration Appeal Board. She was a very astute woman who had a lot of experience in immigration as well as citizenship.

April 13, 1976
Citizenship Act
One of the members of the committee at that time spoke about providing leave to appeal to an immigrant before deportation. His argument was that landed immigrants or prospective landed immigrants should have the right of leave to appeal. The chairperson of the Immigration Appeal Board very wisely contradicted him and pointed out by means of a very good analogy that this certainly is not the case. She used the analogy of a gate to the yard before one even enters the house. She said there is nothing stopping anyone from knocking at the gate to ask permission to enter the yard and then to enter the house. That is the right of every prospective immigrant who comes to this country. We always want to adopt a welcoming attitude to immigrants. But there is no right to enter, just as there is no right for anyone to enter upon your personal property or enter your private home. Entering the yard or entering the home is more a privilege, not a right.
So I ask, Mr. Speaker, why does the minister insist that citizenship is a right when it contradicts the very process by which an applicant gains citizenship? If it is a right, why go through this whole process? It seems to me that the host country, Canada, has the right, indeed the obligation, to examine each applicant and to refuse those she chooses not to accept.
The minister went on to add in his statement:
As a corollary to this second great principle of citizenship as a right we have built into the law the possibility of forgiveness of certain conditions at certain times. The main reasons for this is that I and my predecessors responsible for Canada's citizenship law have, through the years, received letters from unfortunate people who have somehow got tangled up in the machinery of government through no fault of their own or the circumstances of whose birth and subsequent movements around the world have been such that no framers of law could have predicted.
I will readily concede, Mr. Speaker, that under any kind of system or law, circumstances might arise which would bring about unfortunate results for some applicants who apply for citizenship.
The minister is reserving unto himself the right of forgiveness. As the amendment I am proposing tonight points out, the minister has already taken away that right at this point from the judges. They are not supposed to make any assessments of character of applicants who appear before them. The minister wants to have that privilege go in the opposite direction. If there is someone who feels he has been unjustly treated by the process, he wants the opportunity to forgive him some of those things that would hinder his becoming a citizen. He wants to be granted that privilege, and I suppose that is his right as a minister of the Crown. At the same time, why take away some of the prerogatives of judges who are now performing a very good and useful function? As a matter of fact this could take away some of the burdens from the minister in the later stages of the application.
The minister went on to say that the bill gives him certain limited powers of forgiveness, and gives to the governor in council the power to help people for compassionate reasons. He then assures us that this latter power will be used with great care. I have become somewhat cynical of this kind of assurance. It is not good enough for me to have a minister tell me that he promises not to abuse

these powers but that they will be used with great care. If that is the case, then why not outline these powers within the act so that we know exactly how the minister is going to use them?
We have all too many examples in our country of people who have come here not for the welfare of Canada but for selfish or spurious reasons, not thinking of the good of our country at all. I am thinking especially of one who gained national notoriety about a year ago, a man by the name of Hardial Baines, an openly avowed Marxist. He came to this country 16 years ago, he is a landed immigrant, he applied for citizenship and was refused, but is still in the country. He openly speaks of the need for people to revolt against the capitalistic form of government. Are we to forgive that kind of man? Why is he still in the country? There is no measure in this bill or in the Immigration Act that provides powers to deport those people who have gained landed immigrant status, who have been refused citizenship, and who remain in the country. Nothing of that sort is in here.
The minister went on to say that this issue is one that quite frankly surprises him, referring to this reduction in residence requirement from five to three years. Why this should surprise him I do not know, unless he has been speaking only to those people in Peterborough or some areas of Toronto. I assure you that is not the unanimous opinion across Canada. As a matter of fact in my last mailing to my constituency I had as one of my questions whether they felt in their opinion the citizenship requirements as to residence should be reduced from five to three years. While I have not finished the entire tally, I can tell you that even on a partial tally the response has been two and a half to one in favour of maintaining the five-year limit.
Members in the House will perhaps realize from the questions I have asked in this Chamber that I have a lot of immigrants in my riding, people who have come to Surrey-White Rock within the last two or three years. These people are saying we should keep this at five years. In fact I have had letters suggesting it should be seven. I think there are some very sound reasons for maintaining the five-year residence requirement. Let me take a minute or two just to rehearse some of these reasons for the edification of the minister who is here tonight.

speechtext: Why don't you move an amendment?

speechtext:
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) would like me to move an amendment. That just might come, but I would assure the hon. member that he does not need to promptjus for too long to get that kind of amendment.
The minister says there are some people who are ready to become citizens within three years. I do not deny that. There are a good many people who are ready for citizenship within three years. In fact there are some who are ready as soon as they arrive, and no one would deny that. Some people who have fled from very authoritarian governments felt the breath of freedom as soon as their feet touched the shores of Canada. They are thoroughly in love with the democratic system as we enjoy it here, and are ready for citizenship as soon as they come. If they are ready when they arrive and ready three years later, surely
April 13, 1976

they will still be ready in five years time. Those are the very people who appreciate citizenship so much and appreciate being members of the Canadian family to such an extent they are completely willing, perhaps inpatient at times, to wait five years before officially becoming Canadian citizens.
There was a time when immigrants coming to Canada were predominantly from Commonwealth countries. They were thoroughly familiar with the kind of parliamentary system as we practise it here, and as it is practised in other Commonwealth countries. It is completely understandable that those people from Commonwealth nations would be so familiar with our form of government as to be ready for citizenship within five years and, conceivably, ready within three years or less. The pattern of immigration has changed very much in the last decade and we can no longer assume that the majority of the people coming to our shores are familiar with our form or government.

speechtext:
After I have completed my speech I would entertain a question. Mr. Speaker, I will show you that really I have not been moving away from the amendment. It really is apropos of what I have been saying. I was relating to the fact that the minister wants to give half credit to people who have been here in this country before they are here officially as landed immigrants.
We have had experience in the last decade in respect of people who have been here unofficially or without permission before they received landed immigrant status. The minister himself alluded to such cases. In the last decade thousands of people have illegally come to Canada. I might refer to the American draft dodgers who in many cases may have been fine, upright, and upstanding young men. However, they were here illegally.
While these people were here they were granted landed immigrant status in one fell swoop and, presto, chango, they were legitimate residents. According to this bill in three years they would qualify to become citizens. I suggest that although there may have been some very fine prospective citizens among those thousands of people who came to Canada, at the same time there may have been many of them whose reasons for coming to Canada we do not know. Were those reasons spurious; were they legitimate? Were these genuine conscientious objectors, or were they afraid of war, or were they here because their parents did not want them to go to Viet Nam? They were here illegally, but it was not long after they were here illegally that they became legitimate landed immigrants.
According to the bill before us there is no process by which the judge can assess whether or not the person appearing before him should qualify. According to this bill, with the deletions of the minister, the judge does not have the prerogative to examine a particular applicant to deter-

April 13, 1976
Citizenship Act
mine whether or not he should be admitted to Canada as a citizen. This is the matter which I believe must be raised. For this reason I believe the amendment I have submitted to the House should be considered. I believe it is a sound amendment. We need to give the judges the kind of authority that will ensure that the people who come to Canada and become part of our family are the kind of people who are here because they are interested in our country.
Many things have changed in the last few years that have induced people to come to Canada. We know that for the first 100 years, or for the first 200 years of the life of our nation there were thousands of people who came to Canada because they saw it as a land of opportunity, because of all the advantages it would provide for them- the freedom that exists here, the opportunities there would be for their children and their grandchildren, and the economic possibilities. Then within the last 60 years events around the world changed the nature of immigration. The seven days in Russia in 1917 changed entire immigration patterns around the world because one of the fundamental tenets of the Russian revolution was that there was a need incumbent upon a good communist to export the revolution. One cannot call himself a good communist if he does not in fact militantly try to export the revolution.
I was a member of the committee which studied the green paper on immigration. Hearings were held across Canada. When we were in that great bastion of free enterprise, Edmonton, Alberta, we saw, as we did in other cities, demonstrations in front of the hotel where the meetings were held. These were demonstrations by members of the Maoist organization.

It was to be organized at the office of the Company of Young Canadians in Edmonton, an organization which this minister was supporting in his budget until a few months ago.
I suggest there are men and women who want to become citizens of Canada who are not necessarily men and women of good character who are here for our interests. They are not interested in the welfare of Canada. The committee on energy went to the northland. It visited Yellowknife. There the members of the committee met a couple of workers who were working very piously for the members of the Dene nation, supported by Mr. Mel Watkins and also supported by the Secretary of State. He was there supporting the Dene nation. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, we have not heard the last of that.
I am simply illustrating the fact that not everybody who comes to Canada necessarily is thinking of the welfare of this country when he does come here. We need to provide for the judge the kind of power that will give him the authority to make a decision concerning whether or not such a person should be admitted even though on paper, as

the minister suggests, he meets all the qualifications. There ought to be some way in which the judge would be able to decide right there and then whether this person will contribute to the welfare or to the harm of our nation.
I would recommend to the House the acceptance of this amendment because I think it is a good and wholesome step in order that we might ensure the preservation of a Canada that will be integrated, harmonious, and co-operative, and which will provide for us a reservoir of citizens who will look out for our welfare.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to commend the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) for moving the amendment to Bill C-20. I intend to make some comments on the amendment. Throughout the debate on Bill C-20 one of the underlying factors which has affected the thinking of many hon. members is that Canada has been a receiving country of immigrants for the last number of years, with an average immigration of approximately 200,000 per year, so the question of how a person who wants to become a Canadian citizen can become one is a little critical. In the debates at second reading and during committee stage frequent comparisons were made with other countries, especially in view of the reduction of the residency requirement from five years down to something less, in this case, three years. Comparisons were made with countries which have very few immigrants. Those countries are not considered receiving countries.
During the debate at second reading and at committee stage a number of people wrote to me and, I imagine, to other hon. members as well, expressing the fear that we are moving toward a bureaucratic citizenship, or what some referred to as rubber stamp citizenship. When the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) appeared before the committee he gave a fair amount of attention to the fact that once certain conditions and requirements are fulfilled, citizenship is a right. I think this is also an area in which we disagree, not only with regard to immigration but also with regard to citizenship.
Many of us feel that immigration and citizenship are privileges which are bestowed upon individuals by this country. Granted, there are certain conditions whereby an immigrant can come into Canada. There are conditions whereby a landed immigrant can become a citizen. I accept that, but I prefer the system where judges grant citizen-
April 13, 1976

ship only after certain qualifications have been met, including the qualification of good character. I am fearful that we are moving toward an across the counter citizenship, or as some people have said, rubber stamp citizenship.
I should like to come directly to the amendment, which reads as follows:
(f) in the opinion of a citizenship judge, is not shown to be of other than good character.
In his presentation to the committee on February 24 the minister suggested that the qualification of good character was too hard to determine. In other words, there is not a set norm, and therefore, it being arbitrary, he felt that that consideration should be removed from the legislation. The argument was that it was too arbitrary, too subjective, and that the evaluation simply would not stand up in a court of law. I believe those were the three arguments the minister made to us at that time. He also mentioned that with regard to the question of good character an applicant could be refused citizenship, to use the example quoted by the minister, if he towed a person on water skis without another person keeping watch, which is a criminal offence. After that conviction the qualification of good character could be judged as not having been fulfilled and the application at least held in abeyance. On the other hand I think there is some merit in the suggestion that at the present time violations of the Criminal Code or the Narcotic Control Act should be retained.
I think this amendment also addresses itself to the problem of good character, which is just another extrapolation of the provisions as they presently stand in the bill. I gave this concept a fair amount of thought, and I also had difficulty on how to judge good character. I suppose we all have our own standards, but to my mind that condition should remain. A citizenship judge who has been given the responsibility to evaluate people, once the criteria in the act have been established, should be able to make the judgment.
There was very interesting testimony given in the committee, and one person who appeared before the committee expressed it rather well. He might not have had an exhaustive list of good character traits, but I will refer to the testimony which was given before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts on Thursday, March 4.
This testimony was given by, I believe, a constituent of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), who has been a very strong proponent of the bill and who does not like the arbitrary concept of good character. The witness gave a very good definition of how this condition would work. The person was Mr. J. Carraro, director of social services for the Labourers International Union of North America, local 183. Mr. Carraro was a strong supporter of the provision in Bill C-20 wherein the five year residency requirement is reduced to three years. I will be very frank about this. On the one hand I am quoting him, but I will freely admit that on the other hand he thought the requirement could be reduced to three years. At that time I said to him that if the conditions he placed before the committee were embodied in the legislation, I would much better understand the validity of the argument of the minister regarding the reduction from five years to three years.
Citizenship Act
However, that is another matter, and we can address ourselves to that at third reading.
Specifically on the question of good character Mr. Carraro said that his union held citizenship classes. They tried to teach people-I take it primarily of Italian background-their rights in Canada, but very strong emphasis was also placed on the responsibilities which we have in a parliamentary democracy such as Canada. I was very impressed with the testimony of Mr. Carraro and the sincerity with which he tried to answer the questions we put to him.
He had some specific recommendations to make on what he thought should be done in order to make the Citizenship Act and the citizenship procedure more equitable for those with landed immigrant status who wanted to become Canadians through the citizenship procedure.
Quoting from page 38:6 of the committee proceedings, Mr. Carraro said:
Finally, I would like to read some recommendations:
1. That in examining the suitability of an applicant for Canadian citizenship, the judge give priority to the personal and family habits of the applicant over the knowledge of the language and geography of this country.
I had the opportunity, as did a number of other members on the committee, to question Mr. Carraro on how he would define those conditions which he names, such as personal and family habits, as part of the good character clause which he wanted to see retained in the new citizenship act. In response to a question on how he would define good character, Mr. Carraro's list was not exhaustive, but here is what he said. I am quoting from the minutes of the same meeting at page 38:7: He said:
What I would look for is whether a man-let us speak of a man in this case-is a steady worker. I feel that is an objective measure for good character. He is contributing with his work to the betterment of the society. He is a good provider. I think that is good measurable character criterion for good character. Also, whether he is paying his mortgages on time. I think that is also a good character.
I thought that here was a person who had gone through the immigration procedure, had applied for citizenship, had appeared before a Canadian citizenship court and a Canadian citizenship judge, had become a citizen, and now was using his abilities and his association with immigrants to try to teach them the responsibilities and rights that each one of them would enjoy once he becomes a Canadian citizen. I think it was a practical illustration of what one person thought, having gone through the procedure relatively recently, spelled out good character.
It is a pretty practical approach, and while we might not want to incorporate into the act a provision which states that if a person pays his mortgage he should get his citizenship and if he does not pay his mortgage he should not, I do believe that here is a gentleman who was trying to establish for the committee that there are certain acceptable norms of behaviour which we expect from Canadian citizens. He was simply showing to the committee that surely a citizenship judge with certain responsibilities under the act can judge good character or, to make it easier perhaps, he can definitely see when the person before him is not of good character.

April 13, 1976
Citizenship Act
What will happen under the new act is that the judge will not now have the judgmental ability to assess what has been the accommodation of the applicant to Canadian life. I believe that this is especially valid in view of the fact that Bill C-20 will reduce the residency requirements from five years to three.
While some people will argue that this provision is arbitrary, I believe that this type of evaluation takes place every day. It takes place in our courts every day, and I think the minister should take a hard second look at whether or not the quality of good character should be reintroduced into Bill C-20.
I intend to speak again on third reading on other provisions of the bill, but I want to impress upon the minister and his colleagues that while he might argue that it is a subjective evaluation, it is one that has widespread support and one that takes place on a daily basis in the courts of this land. Our judges, having the responsibilities and qualifications that they do, are well capable of using a good character clause. Not only do they feel they are capable of using the parameters which the good character amendment would bring to this bill, not only are they capable of evaluating candidates, but they feel the good caracter clause should be reincorporated in the act to give them the judicial scope which they require at present.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address myself to the amendment which attempts to retain good character as one of the criteria for qualifying for citizenship of this country. I suggest that it becomes essential to talk about some of the other criteria in order to plead for the retention of this one because so much has been lost and is being lost in the bill when citizenship is considered a right rather than a privilege if certain criteria are met. It becomes absolutely essential when we read two excerpts from the minister's statement in the committee when the bill was first discussed there. He said:
What makes this bill unique and a leader among nationality laws of the world? First, it treats absolutely everyone equally. An applicant is an applicant, whether the person be male or female, young or old, from Austria or Australia. This quality is rare in citizenship law.
Then he spoke about citizenship as a right, and eventually about the possibility of the time limit and the language requirement. He said that some citizens will of course have an advantage when they come to this country. He added:
It is to recognize the fact that some people are ready to try to meet the qualifications for citizenship more quickly than others. It is as simple as that. It only takes a moment's thought to realize that an applicant who already speaks one of Canada's two languages, has close family connections within Canada, is familiar with the Canadian form of government, has visited the country, and so on, has tremendous advantages over people who came from a country where they speak neither of the languages, which has a totally different form of government and so forth. There is certainly no guarantee that a person will receive citizenship after three years.
I submit that there is a contradiction in these two statements. It cannot be one and the other at the same time. I suggest that if this bill treats everyone equally it means that the criteria have to go. The criteria used to be five years of residence, security, knowledge, language, character, and something called "other" that I gather is judicial discretion.

Certainly security had some play around 1951, and I suspect the trial which was started off by Igor Gouzenko had something to do with security being a factor when this nation lost the innocence it had acquired through World War II and the hope that we would live in peace forever after. But I gather that the minister was very young in 1950 and has somehow retained his innocence and believes that now in 1976 we live in the same euphoria in which we lived in the years immediately following the war.
This is the time of detente, and security is gone-it was not used in 1974-75. Knowledge is gone as well. It did not matter in 1961, and in the last six years on record only one person a year has failed to acquire citizenship because of lack of knowledge of this country, and that was after five years of possibility for study. Language has been a factor but will cease to be.
There were attempts to amend the bill in order to eliminate the adequate knowledge of one or the other of the official languages. If you are going to treat everyone absolutely equally whether they come from Austria or from Australia, language will have to go and will not be able to stand as a criterion for rejecting a citizenship application. So we are left with character as a factor.
It was hoped that character would play some role in distinguishing between the applicant who failed and the one who succeeded, even though the time of residency was reduced. It seems to me that it is easier to disguise lack of good character for three years than for five years. In five years basic character becomes apparent. It is difficult to hide it for that length of time. But no, we are to reduce the waiting period to three years.
I am not at all convinced that granting citizenship at the end of a three-year period is good. I cannot understand why the government wishes to do this, after wishing to remove all traces of British subject status. Today we put in motion provisions which will eliminate all traces of the British subject from the elections act, as if it were a taint. The provision is to be removed. Some people who have lived in this country many years will not be able to vote at the next election because they will not have applied in time for Canadian citizenship. Is that how the governments means to demonstrate the value of Canadian citizenship? I submit that the value will go down.
In this busy world, time represents value. Actually it represents more than money. If you reduce the waiting period, you reduce the value of citizenship. I suppose it is too much to expect the government, which has reduced the value of our money to 40 per cent of what it was, to make the value of citizenship greater than 40 per cent of its original value.
I have been sent a great many letters in recent days. People write to me about the gun laws, that other infamous bill being put through by the government, and about the death penalty. A common thread runs through the letters, a desire to retain something worth while in this country, to protect this country. Some feel that this country is threatened. I wonder what people like this have been doing in the past year when the government has moved deliberately and cynically to reduce the value of Canadian citizenship.
April 13, 1976

Why will people not rise to the defence of something so worth while as citizenship? What has the Committee for an Independent Canada been doing? What has happened to the professors' report on Canadian studies in Canadian universities? What happened to that report this past year, when this bill was working its way through parliament? Thomas Symons said that there are few other countries in the world which have developed a post-secondary educational system that pays so little attention to the study of the country's own culture in the university curriculum.
We shall require that prospective citizens learn the language, attain a job, and reach some measure of self-sufficiency. We do not require that they shall spend enough time to learn something about our culture and about the essential factors of the country. Why bother stressing the value of citizenship if it can be so easily attained?
I know that in this last-ditch struggle we shall meet with no more success than our amendments met with in committee. We wanted to amend the provisions governing the time factor. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said, "Move an amendment." I moved an amendment in committee, but it received, I am afraid, short shrift from the government that was bent on building a monument to the minister rather than on the retention of the value of citizenship.
In closing, I wonder what is the attitude of those who have sought a Canadian identity and who endeavour to inculcate the Canadian identity in our universities and in the economic systems of this land. I say, to paraphrase the old song:
Yet Hurtigs and ye Symons,
Oh, where hae ye been?
When they gave away the citizenship for Half of what it's been.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief and non-provocative. I hope sincerely that we can read this bill the third time tomorrow, and I shall not do anything which may upset that hope.
I admit that at the committee stage there were genuine differences of opinion between myself and certain hon. members opposite who served on the committee, on the question of good character. One can say that we will agree to disagree. We both stand for principles we are trying to defend.
Hon. members opposite know my concern about good character and know I am not trying to promote bad character. They know, as the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) was good enough to say, that I consider a good character provision as too subjective. It is not measurable in law. I feel that in a piece of legislation like this we should try to avoid subjective provisions of that kind which are, as has been said, interpreted by individuals according to their own views, culture, background, and traditions.
We are not avoiding the issue. We propose to replace the good character provision with a provision which can be measurable in law, namely, one to do with indictable offences. This provision is found in clause 20, which reads in part:
Citizenship Act
Notwithstanding anything in this act, a person shall not be granted citizenship under section 5 or subsection 10(1) or administered the oath of citizenship (a) while he is
(i)	under a probation order,
(ii)	a paroled inmate, or
(iii)	confined in or an inmate of any penitentiary, gaol, reformatory
or prison,
pursuant to any enactment in force in Canada;
And now comes the especially pertinent part, the provision which takes the place of the good character provision:
(b) while he is charged with, on trial for, subject to or a party to an appeal relating to an offence under subsection 28(1) or (2) of an indictable offence under any Act of Parliament.. .
I do not think we can reconcile our differences. It is my contention that the government's approach is measurable in law. I am not proposing anything inconsistent with the spirit of the law. I think this provision makes more sense than retaining the notion of good character. I made the point several times in committee. I have not been able to persuade hon. members opposite; nor have they been able to persuade me.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cyril Symes (Sault Ste. Marie) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
motion No. 2:
-That Bill C-20, An Act respecting citizenship, be amended in Clause 18 by deleting sub-clauses (2), (3) and (4) and substituting the following therefor:
"(2) The Minister shall appoint a tribunal consisting of a Superior Court Judge or Judges who may review any declaration made by the Governor in Council pursuant to sub-section (1) hereof.
(3)	Upon an application for such a review the Minister shall advise the applicant of the particulars of the grounds upon which the Governor in Council has declared that to grant citizenship or issue a certificate of renunciation would be prejudicial to the security of Canada or contrary to public order in Canada, without disclosing the names of witnesses or sources of this information.
(4)	The tribunal shall hold a hearing at which the applicant and the Minister shall be entitled to be present or to be represented by Counsel.
(5)	The tribunal shall make recommendations to the Minister as to whether the declaration by the Governor in Council should be imple-

April 13, 1976
Citizenship Act
mented or withdrawn as the case may be and shall state its reasons
therefor in writing to the applicant and the Minister.
(6)	A declaration made under sub-section (1) ceases to have effect
two years after the day on which it was made.".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to present this amendment at the report stage of this bill because I think the committee, having spent a good part of two sessions dealing with it, recognizes the importance of the problem that relates to the amendment I have moved.
Basically the situation is that in the bill we have before us there is a provision in clause 18 whereby the governor in council, in practice the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), can deny an applicant Canadian citizenship on the grounds that to grant the application would be prejudicial to the security of Canada or contrary to public order in Canada.
That is an important clause in the bill. I do not argue with it being there. It is important that the minister have that discretionary power to deny citizenship because of security reasons, as so stated. What I take exception to is that there is no provision in this bill, nor has there been in the past, that when a minister denies an applicant citizenship for security reasons that those reasons have to be explained to the applicant. Nor does the applicant have an opportunity to appeal those reasons or present to the minister contrary evidence and argument, in other words to have his day in court.
As it stands, the clause seems to be a denial of natural justice. It is a denial to the applicant to be given clearly the reasons for rejecting his citizenship and the opportunity to put forth counter-argument. That is why I have moved the amendment that is before us.
The amendment does not remove the minister's discretionary power to turn down a citizenship applicant for security reasons. Nor does it force the minister to disclose the sources from which he has received the information that led him to conclude the applicant would be a security risk. What the amendment would do is set up an appeal tribunal consisting of superior court judges. It would allow the applicant to see the reasons why he is being denied citizenship without disclosing the sources.
This would provide an applicant with a change to dispute those reasons and present evidence that may contradict some of the arguments the minister has received from his sources. I submit that the confidentiality of the sources of the minister would be maintained. That is important. If security agencies want to continue to receive information from sources, obviously the confidentiality of those must be protected.
I have therefore designed an amendment which I think is reasonable and moderate. It does not demand that the cases be held in open court under normal legal practices. It at least allows the applicant some opportunity for a hearing, although it is a very limited hearing. As it is now without this amendment, a person is simply told he has been denied citizenship for security reasons. They are not enumerated or elaborated. Nor does he have a chance to challenge that decision.
I submit that the amendment I have moved falls in line with general government policy or at least with some of the recommendations made in 1969 by the Royal Commis-

sion on Security which recognized the very problem I have described, namely, that there is a denial of natural justice without this right of appeal. That royal commission made what I thought was a very sensible recommendation. I quote from page 301 of the abridged report:
We recommend that the grant of citizenship should normally be refused on security grounds only if actual illegalities or criminal acts have been committed and proved in court, and not merely for membership in subversive associations or even the communist party. However, we recommend that ministerial discretion should be retained to deal with certain cases in which it may remain appropriate to withhold citizenship for particularly significant security reasons. All persons whose applications are rejected on security grounds should have access to the Security Review Board.
Because the royal commission stated that no group in Canada has been designated as subversive, if someone is going to be denied citizenship on that ground he should have the right of appeal. The royal commission recommended that a security review board be set up. Seven years have passed since that recommendation was put forward. We still have many applicants for Canadian citizenship being turned down for security reasons without any opportunity to appeal that decision. My amendment falls in line with the conclusions of a royal commission.
I do not accept the arguments that we heard in committee from the minister's officials. They stated that the problem is so difficult that the government cannot come up with some kind of security review board or appeal tribunal at this time. They further said it was beyond their mental capacity to design such a board that would guarantee a right of appeal and at the same time protect the minister's discretionary power and confidentiality of sources. If we do not make a move at this time to set up some kind of appeal procedure, how much longer must we wait?
The royal commission made some very important conclusions in 1969 and we should be acting on them. If that royal commission is not enough to convince hon. members of the importance of having this kind of review procedure, I draw their attention to a case that was brought before the Federal Court of Canada in 1973 by an applicant who had been turned down for security reasons. He was not given any argument or any chance to appeal. He took the then Secretary of State to court. I wish to read the decision of the Federal Court judges because I think their conclusions are very relevant and appropriate to my amendment.
The case was T. Lazarov v. Secretary of State of Canada. I read from the decision of Mr. Justice Thurlow of that case in 1973. He stated:
Whenever the reason for contemplating refusal of an application is one that is peculiar to the particular applicant the nature of citizenship and its importance to the individual are such that the applicant ought at least to have an opportunity of some kind and at some stage of the proceedings to dispute its existence.
Further, Mr. Justice Thurlow, with two other justices concurring, ruled that:
The status of citizenship carries with it rights and advantages and to refuse the application of a person to whom it would otherwise be granted on the basis of matters of which he is not apprised and which he is given no opportunity to dispute is shocking to one's sense of justice even though he may lawfully apply again after a comparatively short time. It suggests that the applicant is not being fairly dealt with and fairness demands that he at least be afforded an opportunity to state his position .. In my opinion, therefore, the rule audi alteram
April 13, 1976

partem applies whenever the minister proposes to excercise his discretion to refuse an application on the basis of facts pertaining to the particular applicant or his application and where he has not already had an opportunity in the course of the proceedings before the Citizenship Court he must be afforded a fair opportunity in one way or another of stating his position with respect to any matters which in the absence of refutation or explanation would lead to the rejection of his application. This is not to say a confidential report or its contents need be disclosed to him but the pertinent allegations which if undenied or unresolved would lead to rejection of his application must, as I see it, be made known to him to an extent sufficient to enable him to respond to them and he must have a fair opportunity to dispute or explain them.
That was the considered opinion of a Federal Court justice in a case which is most pertinent to my amendment. So, Mr. Speaker, we have a royal commission arguing the need for an appeal procedure, and we find a Federal Court justice also stating that an appeal procedure is necessary. I understand that the Department of the Secretary of State is appealing that Federal Court decision before the Supreme Court and that the matter is still unresolved. Nevertheless I feel strongly that there ought to be some kind of appeal procedure provided.
I have heard departmental officials argue that though a person might be denied citizenship for security reasons he can reapply after two years. That is true, but neither the officials nor the police agencies are obliged to prepare a new report or submit new evidence which might be on the side of the applicant. All they have to do is resubmit the original files, and the minister denies the application once again. This process could go on every two years. For his part, the applicant has no opportunity to get hold of the reasons for the denial of his application and produce counter arguments. So the two-year provision is no solution; it only puts the applicant back to square one every two years.
We heard an official in the security branch say he recognized the merit of the appeal procedure but he feared that if any such procedure were introduced the government's sources of information might dry up. I presume he was referring to the RCMP or to police agencies or to organizations such as the FBI or the CIA. But my amendment would take care of such a situation by providing for a hearing in confidence-the reasons need only be stated to the applicant in a general way, and the sources of the information need not be disclosed. Thus there should be no fear on the part of the government that its sources of information would dry up.
I might say, as an aside, that I am rather skeptical and, indeed, highly critical of the government's sources of information if they include the CIA, which has become infamous for its illegal activities, as we saw during the Watergate affair, and for carrying out all kinds of spying for a former president. We should remember that in the United States a law has been passed requiring the FBI and the CIA to present any dossier concerning a person when that person requests it. And these agencies have not gone to ruin because such a basic right has been granted with the object of protecting civil liberty.
I realize the government is preoccupied about the secrecy of information, but in an area such as this which so closely affects natural justice I believe it ought to recognize that my amendment does not, in fact, jeopardize its sources of information. It is of great importance that an applicant should have an opportunity of appearing before a tribunal to hear the evidence and comment upon it.
Citizenship Act
There is historical precedent in Canada for such an amendment as I propose. During the second world war and thereafter, in the course of what I consider to be a sad chapter in Canadian history, when citizens of Japanese origin and other so-called aliens were interned, the government set up an appeal procedure whereby anyone who was to be interned had a right to appeal along the lines I have suggested here. Government sources of information were protected, but at least the person concerned had a right to his day in court, as it were.
When we look at the history of the denial of citizenship on security grounds we cannot but be concerned over what has been happening in recent times. The government has never been obliged to define precisely what is meant by "protecting the security of Canada" or "prejudicial to public order". There are phrases which can be interpreted by bureaucrats and by the government as they go along.
One has only to look at the pattern of denial of citizenship for security reasons to see how irregular the definition of these phrases has been-how it fluctuates from time to time as people interpret the situation according to the vogue of the period. When we look at the statistics provided for us we find that since 1949 2,173 applicants have been denied Canadian citizenship for security reasons. This figure represents 39.9 per cent of the total number of rejections year by year. It is a significant proportion. But when we look at the pattern of the number of rejections in each year something very interesting emerges.
In 1949, 28 people were denied citizenship for security reasons. By 1951 the number had jumped to 170 and remained at about that level, between 150 and 190, from 1951 to 1959. Then it began to drop off, falling to 70 in 1963, and 11 in 1973. Hon. members will notice that the high watermark of rejection occurred during the McCarthy red scare era in the United States which spilled over into Canada as well. There followed a kind of hysteria when people looked for security risks behind every door and in every closet. This shows how unregulated and widely interpreted this concept of a security risk can be.
When we questioned the minister's officials in committee, my confidence that the interpretation would be fair was not in any way strengthened. For example, when I asked them how they interpret "prejudicial to the security of Canada" or "contrary to public order in Canada", Mr. Nichols, as reported at page 44:7 of the minutes for Tuesday, March 23, had this to say:
On the matter of how we will interpret the words of the bill, again I am at a great disadvantage. The words of the bill, as I have said, are simply a phraseology to describe what is now done. The present act does not talk about security. It evolved. Canada has been in the security business regarding the naturalization of aliens since about 1918. Various methods have been used through the years. Most of them just grew.
I suppose they just grew like Topsy, Mr. Speaker. It is something that has evolved without any kind of definition or regulation. I worry when bureacrats make definitions according to their whims and fancies as the days go by. If we are going to have this kind of latitude in interpretation, we must have some appeal procedure to guarantee basic human rights.

April 13, 1976
Citizenship Act
I am not speaking abstractly, Mr. Speaker. I have pointed to figures showing people who have been denied Canadian citizenship for these reasons. I have quoted a court case, and there have been other cases as well. The most current one concerns an individual called Mr. Offley who came to Canada a few years ago. He applied for citizenship which was approved by a citizenship judge, but he was turned down by the minister for security reasons. Because he renounced his U.S. citizenship and cannot get Canadian citizenship, he now finds he is without a country, unable to move out of Canada.
To show in human terms what happens when people are caught up in the regulations, I should like to quote a letter Mr. Offley wrote to the Secretary of State on April 9. In part he said:
Your decision to refuse my application means that I am, and will stay, a permanent domiciled resident in Canada. I am stateless, and thus immune from deportation, as no country will accept me either as a visitor or as an immigrant.
However, if my rejection has no substantial consequences for you, it has quite immense ones for me. It means that my legal status will remain one of living in limbo, with no possibility of gaining citizenship, without even the alternative of leaving. I have been conferred this status without a trial, without access to the allegations on which the decision was taken, without a right to confront my accusers, and without right of appeal. It is a decision that has been taken without reference to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Security and without regard to the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal.
I think that points out in a quiet, dramatic way how this law affects individuals. There may be good reasons for turning down applicants on security grounds; I do not dispute that. Nor do I dispute the minister's right to do so. But surely in this country, which prides itself on its democracy and long tradition of basic human rights, we should at least allow the accused, so to speak, to have his day in court, although in this case it certainly is a rather restricted one because of the circumstances.
We discussed this very thoroughly in committee, and it was my feeling that because members were generally concerned with trying to wrestle with the problem, that they felt deeply about it. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) was very sympathetic and argued that we must move in this direction.
I do not have much hope that government members will support my amendment; it will probably go down to defeat. Nevertheless I wanted to put on record something that concerns me as a Canadian and believer in liberty and justice. I hope my arguments, if they do not move the government to bring in a security review board or appeal procedure at this stage, will give the government added impetus to take action and bring in such a review procedure in the near future.

First of all, we have stated the nature of the discretionary power involved in rather plain language, so that applicants are not refused without reason being given. Secondly, the discretionary act is moved to a higher authority and the decision will be collegial. In other words, it will no longer be a simple act of discretion on the part of the minister but will also involve the governor in council. Thirdly, for the first time we will make available to a refused applicant the reasons for his refusal. He will be told in so many words that he has been refused citizenship for security reasons, and he will be given this information in confidence.
I think that is an improvement over the present situation. I do not think I would argue, though, with a great deal of personal conviction that it answers all the questions that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie raised tonight. I think those will be subject to further reviews down the line.

speechtext:
Motion No. 3: That Bill C-20, An Act respecting citizenship, be amended in Clause 33 by deleting sub-clause 6(e).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be much more brief in my explanation of this amendment. It deals with the amendment proposed by the minister regarding property and how it relates to ownership and citizenship.
Briefly the situation up to now has been that under the constitution the provinces have control over property. What has happened in many provinces, certainly in my
April 13, 1976

povince of Ontario and in Prince Edward Island, has been that foreign ownership of land has become a great problem. Recreation land was bought up by non-Canadians and a lot of land speculation took place. The only way a province could put a stop or a slowdown to this process of foreign ownership and the purchase of land was to pass regulations denying ownership on the basis of non-residency. That is to say, if you wanted to buy land in Prince Edward Island you had to be a resident of Prince Edward Island. This was felt to be rather restrictive. By denying ownership to anyone not a resident, not only do you deny the right of foreign nationals to buy land, you prevent other Canadians from buying land in that province.
What the bill before us does is widen the scope of action on the part of a province. It will allow a province to deny ownership of land on the basis of residency, as has been the case in the past, and also on the basis of citizenship. That it to say, if a province designs the legislation, a non-Canadian would be prohibited from owning certain types of land. Of course I agree with that. What I object to is one clause in the amendment presented by the minister which states that if the Foreign Investment Review Agency, which is a federal agency, decides that an ownership acquisition by a foreign company is in order, then that is to overrule any provincial law which may deny ownership on the basis of non-Canadian citizenship.
I moved an amendment to deal with the clause relating to the Foreign Investment Review Agency for a number of reasons. First of all, it is a fact that many of the provinces object to the clause itself on the basic ground that it is an intrusion of federal jurisdiction into what is clearly defined by the constitution as a provincial right, namely, the right of property. It also means that the rules can be changed at any time because the Foreign Investment Review Act can be amended at any time by the federal government without consultation with the provinces. Some of the provinces, therefore, are in dispute over this clause. Because we did not hear from the witnesses for the provinces at the committee it would be more appropriate to delete this clause until the federal government can talk to the provinces in an attempt to hammer out something agreeable to the majority.
In addition, I think the foreign investment review clause negates the general thrust of the amendment which is intended to broaden the scope under which provinces can act. It may well be that a province might want to deny ownership to a foreign company buying up real estate for land speculation purposes, either on the outskirts of an urban centre or in the urban centre itself, or deny the right of a foreign land corporation to buy up agricultural land, as has been going on in many of the provinces.
We could conceivably have such a foreign company being given the right by the Foreign Investment Review Agency to buy up Canadian companies and the land on which they reside or which they control. This would be contrary to the intent of the amendment, to give the provinces some power to restrict ownership on grounds other than just residency. That is to say, they could restrict ownership on the basis of not being a Canadian citizen.
It is my feeling that it would be best at this time that the clause be deleted for the reasons outlined. I do not wish to go into more detail as we discussed it in committee, but
Citizenship Act
again I felt it was important to put this on the record and I commend my amendment to the House.
