subtopic: TRADE-EFFECT OF REPEAL OF SECTION 272 OF RAILWAY ACT ON FLOUR AND GRAIN EXPORTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
TRADE-EFFECT OF REPEAL OF SECTION 272 OF RAILWAY ACT ON FLOUR AND GRAIN EXPORTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the last should always be first, but I did not know that I would really be first that quickly. I count on you and other people for small mercies. Now to get down to business.
My business in being here tonight is to deal with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) in connection with what I think is a great travesty as it affects the people of Halifax, the people of Saint John, the people of Montreal, the millers in all parts of eastern Canada, and the western grain growers, more particularly those of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I hope I have covered the ground adequately for that with which I intend to deal. This is probably my sixth appearance on the late show in the last three or four weeks in connection with this particular subject.
What concerns me is that the Minister of Transport, who should be the custodian and guardian of Section 272 of the Railway Act, is going to repeal this by virtue of Clause 15 of the bill which is item no. 87 on the current hit parade; that is, the restraint program before us in parliament. That is the reason why I appear here tonight, as I have on a number of occasions, to appeal to the Minister of Transport, my dear friend; the President of the Treasury Board, a dear friend of mine also; the Minister of Agriculture, also a dear friend; and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, also a dear friend. I hope I have proven in previous debate that what they propose will cause a loss to the Canadian economy of at least $100 million a year. Whether we like that or not I think that is an important figure.
I believe I have proven that this has been an ill-contrived program. It is something that not only I will fight but which also will be fought by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax-East (Mr. Forrestall). The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers) also will be dragged into this fight before it is over. There will be 22 or 25 members from the city of Montreal who will be dragged into it, as well as members from the western grain growing areas of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In other words, it will be one hell of a good fight in this House of Commons. I can say without even taking a second breath that that is exactly what will happen. Why will this come about?
Before asking the spokesman for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to reply I will venture to suggest the reason this will come about is simply that when the new Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Humboldt,

took his place he was told that he would have to achieve a certain amount of savings. He went back to his department, which admittedly has been in a mess not only since the days of the minister who preceded him but since the days of a couple of ministers back.
He asked what he could do in order to effect savings in his department. He was told that the flour-grain subsidy could be dealt with because no one would protest it. He was told that it might affect Halifax, Saint John or Montreal, but that the people involved are all very supine and that no one would be smart enough to spot it. The darned trouble was that quite a few people did spot it very quickly. Many of them were very quick to raise a resentful voice. I was one who raised the matter, and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) was another. Between the two of us we batted this thing back and forth for the last couple of weeks. I will tell you, Sir, that I think the new Minister of Transport now realizes this. This does not involve merely the two of us. There are about 20 and probably more members of parliament who are prepared to start raising a very large fuss about what he proposes to do.
This has been scouted thoroughly in the past. I do not wish to go into the fact and figures, but I am prepared to debate the facts and figures in respect of this matter with anyone. The fact is that the Port of Halifax will not be dealt with in the way suggested, nor will the port of Saint John. I may stand as a rather small figure compared to the large number of figures who have not yet spoken in respect of the port of Montreal. Before this is over not only will the members from Montreal be involved is this but also the members from Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the two grain growing provinces.
When we return after Easter there will be a large number of people fighting for what I am fighting for tonight, and I will not feel too much alone at that time. I will be able to say that at least I was a pioneer. What I am fighting for, Mr. Speaker, is that we do not throw out an old policy until we can come in with something new that is better. Until the Minister of Transport does that, I will be fighting for an old policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRADE-EFFECT OF REPEAL OF SECTION 272 OF RAILWAY ACT ON FLOUR AND GRAIN EXPORTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. colleague mentioned that he did not want to be last, he certainly raised a problem that was the subject of many discussions. I personally raised that problem many times in the Department of Transport. When he mentioned the Department of Transport, the Treasury Board and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce as having something to do with this problem, one sees how complex the problem raised by the hon. member is.
The government came under numerous protests for repealing section 272 of the Railway Act. Of course, the decision to eliminate the "At and East" subsidy was made to reduce government expenditures. It may be easy to blame the government for its excessive expenditures-and we hear about it virtually every day during the question period in the House-but it is even a lot more difficult to suggest means of reducing those expenditures without clashes. All budget cuts were made after consultation with the bodies involved and after considering regional submis-
April 13, 1976

sions and needs within an overall policy dealing with socio-economic aspects, or still within an economic policy for the whole of all Canadians.

With respect to the ports of Saint John and Halifax, the Minister of Transport has indicated that the removal of the subsidy may encourage beneficial developments, such as the movement of grain by unit train to these ports.
Flour exports from most traditional exporting countries, including Canada, Australia, and the United States, have been declining for a number of years. This is due to several factors, including a trend toward national self-sufficiency in milling capacity throughout the world. Nonetheless, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce advised the hon. member, he intends to have discussions with the Minister of Transport and his officials on this subject.
I congratulate the hon. member who raised this question, and I assure him that it is very important. I hope the decision will reflect the needs of all Canadians.

subtopic: FINANCE-MONITORING OF INCOME OF INSURANCE AGENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
FINANCE-MONITORING OF INCOME OF INSURANCE AGENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to start on a pleasant note by congratulating the parliamentary secretary for doing double duty this evening and representing the forces of the government in such an adequate and astute way.

subtopic: FINANCE-MONITORING OF INCOME OF INSURANCE AGENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The forces of evil.

subtopic: FINANCE-MONITORING OF INCOME OF INSURANCE AGENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
I didn't say that.
The question I raised several weeks ago was with regard to the increasing evidence that incomes for insurance agents in British Columbia have gone up dramatically as a result of the increase in auto insurance rates in that province. It was not raised out of any petulance or envy of those incomes. It was raised because any anti-inflation program worth the name must develop some kind of consensus within the population, and differences in raises within that population must be seen to be fair for any anti-inflation program to work.
The evidence is that the average rate for auto insurance in British Columbia has doubled, and the charges insurance agents make for collecting those premiums have remained approximately the same. They have reduced their rate from 7 per cent to 5 per cent on the basis of statutory coverage and it has remained 10 per cent on the optional coverage. The collision coverage, which is now optional, goes into that optional area. Let me give you an example.
The commission that an agent would get on a 1973 Toyota between last year and this year has increased by 83 per cent, given the same risk. With the same work force, the same number of people, the same staff, that increase is not justifiable under any kind of meaningful anti-inflation program. As a result of that I decided I would drop a note to the Anti-Inflation Board to see what steps the chairman of that board would be able to take with regard to what
Adjournment Debate
appears to be an excessive increase in the incomes of one section of the community. I should like to quote from a letter from Jean-Luc Pepin, dated March 30, and directed to me in response to my letter. He writes:
Increased earnings derived from direct commission in a guideline year are not subject to legal restraint, providing the formula by which the income is determined does not change from the base to the guideline year.
Later he goes on to state:
The increase in remuneration would be attributed to an increase in productivity.
It is that quote from the letter in which the chairman suggests that somehow the increase in the incomes of insurance agents in British Columbia has something to do with productivity which makes me think that the government is living in an Alice in Wonderland world, and the legislation it has proposed in terms of controlling inflation does nothing meaningful whatsoever with regard to the incomes of such people.
I would like the parliamentary secretary to put himself in the shoes of a lumber worker in my constituency who finds, first, that his wages are frozen; second, that his insurance rates have been tripled; third, that the export levy has been removed on the lumber that his company sells abroad, which means that it can make just as much profit as it likes because it is not under the anti-inflation guidelines; fourth, when he buys his insurance he finds his insurance agent no longer flies to Hawaii every year, he can now go around the world if he likes. That kind of program does not give any hope of a consensus on antiinflation measures. From time to time people in our party are critized as being carping critics, but I am trying to be positive on this.
I hope the parliamentary secretary in responding to this question will deal with what the legislation can do to control this excess of income and will tell us what specific proposals his government is now prepared to make to bring the incomes of professional people and people at that level under some control. I suggest it has to be in the form of income taxation. This should be done so that the people who work with their hands in the mills, who have their wages frozen, and people who are on low incomes can have some confidence that the program is not being carried on their backs, which certainly evidence concerning incomes of insurance agents in British Columbia would seem to support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FINANCE-MONITORING OF INCOME OF INSURANCE AGENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to thank the hon. member for his kind remarks and I hope he will be satisfied with the reply I intend to give him.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) has asked if the income of agents selling insurance on behalf of the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (ICBC) is being monitored under the guidelines of the anti-inflation program. I would note, first of all, that the province of British Columbia and the federal government are in the process of negotiating an agreement under the anti-inflation program. Until such an agreement is signed, none of the provincial public sector, including any of its

April 13, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Crown corporations, is covered under the anti-inflation program.
Second, the minister indicated quite clearly to the provinces on February 10, 1976, in reply to a question on whether the ICBC would be covered by a Canada-B.C. agreement on the anti-inflation program, that we would be quite prepared to discuss the inclusion of provincial agencies under such an agreement. The procedure that has been followed with provinces that have signed an agreement has been to annex to any memorandum of agreement the specific schedule listing such government bodies that are to be covered. The final decision on which bodies will be covered by the government remains with the provinces.
In this regard I wish to bring to your attention Premier Bennett's statement of February 27, 1976, in which he indicated his government's intention to have the national anti-inflation guidelines apply to pricing and compensation decisions in the British Columbia public sector.
With respect to the specific question on monitoring of income of agents of ICBC, it is the minister's understanding that such agents are not salaried employees. They operate under a contractual agreement with ICBC, and are paid on a commission basis. Furthermore, the minister is given to understand that commission rates vary by type of insurance sold. An agent's remuneration would depend, as well, on the size and number of contracts he negotiates.
If such a case were to be brought to the attention of the Anti-Inflation Board, it is the minister's impression that they would be guided by their compensation regulations which provide for review of commission rate structures for those employers subject to monitoring under the program. I would note, however, that the anti-inflation guidelines are not intended to penalize those individuals whose productivity increases. In this case, any increased income of agents which is attributable to an increase in the size and number of contracts they negotiate would be within the guidelines under the anti-inflation program.
